2027-05-02.title: Fifth Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: The Spirit of truth will guide you
Rejoice before the Lord at the feast of weeks
David becomes great, for the Lord was with him
Filled with joy and the Holy Spirit
Seek the things that are above
Your pain will turn into joy
2027-05-02.alt: Season of Qyomtho. The Ascension of our Lord (Suloko) is on Thursday 6 May: remind the faithful.
2027-05-02.verse: So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.
theo: At the Last Supper Jesus prepares his disciples for his going. “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.” They will weep while the world rejoices, “but your pain will turn into joy.” He compares it to a woman in labour: her pain is forgotten in the joy of a child born into the world. The Resurrection is that birth; Christian joy is born through the Cross.

“So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” This is the joy of Qyomtho: not a mood that changes with circumstances, but a gift no one can take away, because it rests on the risen Christ. Acts shows the first disciples, even when expelled from a city, “filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit”.

Jesus promises the Spirit: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” As the Ascension and Pentecost approach, the Church is taught to live not by sight but by the Spirit, who leads her into the fullness of truth. And Jesus teaches us to pray with confidence: “Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.”

St Paul gives the practical consequence: “If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above… Set your minds on things that are above.” Then he lists what must be put to death and what put on. Proverbs adds: “Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offences.” Easter joy shows itself in a changed life.
conn: The feast of weeks.
Deuteronomy 16:10–12: Israel rejoiced fifty days after Passover; Christians count fifty days from Easter to Pentecost.
Labour pains and new birth.
Isaiah 26:17–19 and 66:7–14 speak of birth pangs leading to new life; Jesus applies the image to his Passion and Resurrection.
Joy that cannot be taken.
Acts 13:52: persecution cannot remove the joy of the Spirit.
Things above.
Colossians 3:1: the risen life orients us towards Christ seated at the right hand of God.
altar: “I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice.” Every Holy Qurbono is this seeing again: the risen Lord comes, and our sorrow is turned into joy.
outline: Opening
What steals our joy?
Point 1 · Pain turned into joy
The woman in labour: joy through the Cross.
Point 2 · Joy no one can take
Easter joy rests on Christ, not circumstances.
Point 3 · The Spirit of truth
Preparing for the Ascension and Pentecost.
Point 4 · Seek the things above
A changed life is the sign of Easter joy.
Take-home line
“No one will take your joy from you.”
live: Count your joys
Each evening this week, thank God for three joys of the day.
Ask in his name (John 16:24)
Bring one need to the Father with confidence in Jesus' name.
Come for the Ascension
Attend the Holy Qurbono of the Ascension on Thursday.
fathers: St Augustine
That little while seems long to us while it lasts; when it is over we shall know how little it was. Our joy is now in hope, then it will be in reality (Tractates on John 101).
St Cyril of Alexandria
The pain of the disciples was turned into joy when they saw the Lord risen; so too for us the sufferings of this world will be followed by the joy that no one can take away (Commentary on John 11).
magis: Evangelii Gaudium 1, 6
The joy of the Gospel fills the hearts of those who encounter Jesus; there are Christians whose lives seem like Lent without Easter.
Catechism 1829, 1832
Joy is a fruit of charity and of the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 243, 729
Christ promises the Spirit of truth who will guide the Church into all truth.
saints: Thursday 6 May: Suloko, the Ascension of our Lord; Holy Qurbono for the people. The ten days of prayer for the coming of the Spirit begin.
2027-05-02.prayer: Lord Jesus, you promised that our pain would turn into joy and that no one would take it from us. Send us your Spirit of truth, teach us to ask in your name, and set our hearts on the things that are above, where you are seated at the right hand of the Father. Amen.

2027-05-06.title: Suloko · The Ascension of our Lord
readings: The tablets placed in the ark
Elijah taken up; Elisha takes his mantle
I will write my law on their hearts
He was lifted up, and a cloud took him
He blessed them and was carried up into heaven
2027-05-06.alt: Suloko, the Ascension of our Lord: Holy Qurbono for the people. Ten days of prayer for the coming of the Holy Spirit follow; according to the lectionary, marriages are not celebrated in these days.
2027-05-06.verse: While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.
theo: Forty days after his Resurrection, Jesus leads his disciples out to Bethany, “and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.” The last earthly sight of Jesus is of hands raised in blessing. He goes, but he does not stop blessing his Church.

The Ascension is not Jesus leaving us; it is our humanity entering heaven. The Son of God, who took our flesh, now takes it to the right hand of the Father. St Mark says: “he was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.” Where the Head has gone, the body hopes to follow. Our true home is with him.

The angels ask the disciples: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? This Jesus… will come in the same way as you saw him go.” The Ascension is not a time for gazing at the sky but for mission: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation… And they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them.”

As Elijah was taken up and Elisha received his mantle and spirit, so Christ ascends and pours out his Spirit on his Church. Jeremiah's promise will be fulfilled at Pentecost: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts.” Like the disciples, who “returned to Jerusalem with great joy and were continually in the temple blessing God”, we now enter ten days of prayer for the Spirit.
conn: Elijah's mantle.
2 Kings 2:13–15: Elisha takes the mantle of the ascended Elijah and receives his spirit: a figure of the Church receiving Christ's Spirit.
The ark and the law.
Deuteronomy 10:1–5: the tablets placed in the ark; Jeremiah 31:33: the law written on hearts by the Spirit.
Gifts from on high.
Ephesians 4:8–11: the ascended Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to build up his body.
A light to the nations.
Isaiah 49:6 and Acts 1:8: the mission goes to the ends of the earth.
altar: At every Holy Qurbono we are invited: “Lift up your hearts”, and we answer, “They are with the Lord.” The ascended Christ, seated at the Father's right hand, comes down to us on the altar, and lifts us up to him.
outline: Opening
Hands raised in blessing: the last sight of Jesus.
Point 1 · Our humanity in heaven
Where the Head has gone, the body will follow.
Point 2 · Why stand looking up?
Ascension leads to mission.
Point 3 · Elijah's mantle
The Spirit given to the Church.
Point 4 · Ten days of prayer
With Mary and the apostles, waiting for Pentecost.
Take-home line
“Lift up your hearts.”
live: Keep the ten days
Pray each day until Pentecost: “Come, Holy Spirit.”
Go and tell (Mark 16:15)
Share the Good News with one person this week, in word or deed.
Lift up your heart
At the Qurbono, really lift up your heart to the Lord at “Lift up your hearts”.
fathers: St Leo the Great
“Christ's Ascension is our elevation; where the glory of the Head has gone before, there the hope of the body is called to follow” (Sermon 73 on the Ascension, 4).
St Augustine

“Today our Lord Jesus Christ ascended into heaven; let our hearts ascend with him… He did not leave heaven when he came down to us; nor did he withdraw from us when he went up again into heaven” (Sermon on the Ascension, Mai 98).
magis: Catechism 659–667
Christ's Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus' humanity into God's heavenly domain; he precedes us so that we might live in hope of following.
Catechism 1137–1139
The heavenly liturgy: the ascended Christ is the high priest of the true sanctuary.
Catechism 2623
The disciples, with Mary, persevered in prayer awaiting the Spirit.
saints: Sunday 9 May: VI Sunday after Qyomtho. Sunday 16 May: Pentecost.
2027-05-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, ascended into heaven, you raised your hands to bless your disciples and took our humanity to the Father's right hand. Bless us from heaven, lift up our hearts to you, send us to proclaim your Gospel, and pour out your Spirit on your Church. Amen.

2027-05-09.title: Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: I am the Lord; I will free you
Your immortal spirit is in all things
I have swept away your sins like a cloud
The eyes of your heart enlightened
It is to your advantage that I go away
2027-05-09.alt: Sunday between the Ascension and Pentecost. In the 2025–26 lectionary this was Social Communication Media Day. Remind the faithful about Pentecost next Sunday.
2027-05-09.verse: It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.
theo: Between the Ascension and Pentecost the Church lives in the upper room. The apostles, “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus”, are “constantly devoting themselves to prayer.” Jesus has gone to the Father; the Spirit has not yet come. It is a time of waiting, but not of emptiness: it is the Church at prayer, gathered around Mary.

Jesus had told them: “It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.” His physical presence was limited to one place; the Spirit will make him present everywhere, in every heart and every altar. The Spirit “will prove the world wrong about sin and righteousness and judgment”: he convicts, converts and gives courage.

In the evening Gospel we hear the beginning of Jesus' great priestly prayer: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you… And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” The ascended Christ continues this prayer for us at the Father's right hand.

God says to Joshua as he takes up Moses' task: “Be strong and courageous; do not be frightened or dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.” St Paul prays that “with the eyes of your heart enlightened, you may know what is the hope to which he has called you.” Let us spend this week like the apostles: in prayer, with Mary, waiting for the Spirit.
conn: The upper room.
The room of the Last Supper becomes the room of waiting and of Pentecost (Acts 1:13; 2:1).
Mary at prayer.
Mary, overshadowed by the Spirit at the Annunciation, prays with the Church for the Spirit's coming (Acts 1:14).
Joshua after Moses.
As Joshua received Moses' charge, the apostles receive Christ's mission; the same promise: “I will be with you.”
Sins swept away.
Isaiah 44:22: the forgiveness the Spirit brings when he convicts the world of sin.
altar: At every Holy Qurbono the Church does what the apostles did in the upper room: gathered with Mary and the saints, she prays for the Spirit, and the Spirit comes upon the gifts and upon us.
outline: Opening
Waiting: between Ascension and Pentecost.
Point 1 · Better that I go
The Spirit makes Christ present everywhere.
Point 2 · The upper room
The Church at prayer with Mary.
Point 3 · Be strong and courageous
Joshua's charge for our mission.
Point 4 · Eternal life is to know God
The priestly prayer of Jesus.
Take-home line
“Come, Holy Spirit.”
live: A Pentecost novena
Pray each day until Pentecost for one gift of the Holy Spirit.
Pray with Mary
Pray the Rosary this week with the intention of a new Pentecost in your family.
Use media well
Share something good and true online this week; avoid sharing gossip or anger.
fathers: St Augustine

It was expedient for them that the form of a servant be taken from their sight, so that, no longer clinging to the flesh, they might love him spiritually and receive the Spirit (Tractates on John 94).
St Cyril of Alexandria
Christ had to depart in the flesh so that the Spirit might dwell in us; through the Spirit Christ himself is with us (Commentary on John 10).
magis: Catechism 729–730
Only when the hour of his glorification had come did Jesus promise the coming of the Spirit; the Spirit will be with us for ever.
Catechism 726
Mary, filled with the Holy Spirit, is present with the apostles at the dawn of the last times.
Inter Mirifica 3 / Aetatis Novae
The Church sees the means of social communication as gifts of God to be used for the good.
saints: The days of prayer for the Holy Spirit continue. Sunday 16 May: Pentecost.
2027-05-09.prayer: Lord Jesus, you went to the Father so that the Advocate might come. Gather us with Mary and the apostles in prayer, make us strong and courageous, enlighten the eyes of our hearts, and send your Holy Spirit upon your Church. Amen.

2027-05-16.title: The Sunday of Pentecost
readings: The Advocate will teach you everything
The spirit rests on the seventy elders
The land divided among the tribes
The spirit of God comes upon Saul
A new heart and a new spirit
Varieties of gifts, the same Spirit
Another Advocate, to be with you for ever
2027-05-16.alt: The Sunday of Pentecost: Holy Qurbono for the people. The season of Pentecost begins.
2027-05-16.verse: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.
theo: “When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place. And suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind… Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit.” Fifty days after Easter, the promise of the Father is fulfilled. The Church, gathered in prayer with Mary, receives the Spirit and is born into mission.

The crowds from every nation hear the apostles “in our own languages… speaking about God's deeds of power.” At Babel human pride scattered the nations in confusion of tongues; at Pentecost the Spirit gathers them in one faith, each hearing in his own language. The Church is catholic from her first day: one Spirit, many peoples, many languages, including ours.

The Old Testament readings were longing for this day. Moses wished: “Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit on them!” Ezekiel promised: “A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you… I will put my spirit within you.” Now it happens. The Spirit who rested on a few prophets is poured out on all the baptised.

Jesus had promised: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you forever… I will not leave you orphaned.” St Paul explains that the one Spirit gives many gifts, “to each… for the common good.” Each of us received this Spirit in Baptism and Chrismation. Pentecost asks: are we living by the Spirit's power, or as if he had never come?
conn: Babel reversed.
Genesis 11: one language divided by pride; Acts 2: many languages united in praise.
Sinai and Pentecost.
Pentecost was the feast of the giving of the Law at Sinai; now the Law is written on hearts by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:27).
The seventy elders.
Numbers 11: the spirit shared from Moses to the elders; Pentecost: the Spirit given to the whole Church.
Fire.
The burning bush, the pillar of fire, the coal of Isaiah: now tongues of fire on each disciple.
altar: At the epiclesis of every Holy Qurbono the priest calls the Holy Spirit upon the bread and wine and upon the people. Every Qurbono is a little Pentecost: the same Spirit who came upon the apostles makes Christ present and makes us one body.
outline: Opening
Wind and fire in the upper room.
Point 1 · The promise fulfilled
Another Advocate, for ever: we are not orphans.
Point 2 · Babel reversed
One Spirit, many languages: the Church for all nations.
Point 3 · A new heart
Ezekiel and Moses: the Spirit poured on all.
Point 4 · Gifts for the common good
Discover and use your gifts in the Church.
Take-home line
“Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful.”
live: Renew your Chrismation
Thank God for the Spirit received with holy Myron at Baptism; pray “Come, Holy Spirit” daily.
Use one gift
Offer one gift you have (music, teaching, care, skill) to your parish this month.
Speak the language of love
Be reconciled with someone with whom you “don't speak the same language”.
fathers: St Irenaeus of Lyons

The Spirit descended at Pentecost, having power to admit all nations to life; he brought the scattered tribes to unity and offered to the Father the first fruits of all nations (Against Heresies III, 17, 2).
St Cyril of Jerusalem
The Spirit comes gently, like rain on dry ground; one water becomes the lily's whiteness and the rose's red; so the one Spirit works in each as he wills (Catechetical Lectures 16, 12).
magis: Catechism 731–732
On the day of Pentecost the Passover of Christ is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; the Holy Trinity is fully revealed.
Catechism 1287–1288
The Spirit given at Pentecost is communicated to the baptised through the sacrament of Chrismation (Confirmation).
Catechism 799–801
Charisms are graces of the Spirit for the building up of the Church.
saints: Friday 21 May: Golden Friday (Acts 3:1–10, the healing at the Beautiful Gate). 26 May: St Philip Neri.
2027-05-16.prayer: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love. As you came upon the apostles with Mary, come upon our families, our parish and our Church: give us a new heart, unite us in one faith, and send us to proclaim the wonders of God. Amen.

2027-05-23.title: First Sunday after Pentecost
readings: The manna ceases; they eat the produce of the land
Filled with the spirit of the Lord
Plans for your welfare, a future with hope
The Bereans examine the Scriptures daily
2027-05-23.alt: Season of Pentecost. In the 2025–26 lectionary this Sunday was Vocation Day.
2027-05-23.verse: By contrast, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
theo: The season of Pentecost is the season of the Church's life in the Spirit. If Pentecost was the planting, these Sundays are about the fruit. St Paul names it: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control… If we live by the Spirit, let us also be guided by the Spirit.”

In the evening Gospel Jesus tells the parable of the sower. Seed falls on the path, on rock, among thorns and on good soil. “As for that in the good soil, these are the ones who, when they hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance.” The Spirit sows; we must become good soil: attentive, deep, free from the thorns of worry and riches.

In the Gospel the crowds follow Jesus after the multiplication of loaves, looking for more bread. He tells them: “Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life.” When they ask what work God wants, he answers: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” “The bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” Israel's manna stopped when they reached the promised land; the true Bread will never fail.

Jeremiah gives a word of hope to people in exile: “I know the plans I have for you, says the LORD, plans for your welfare and not for harm, to give you a future with hope… When you search for me, you will find me; if you seek me with all your heart.” God has a plan, a vocation, for each of us; the Spirit leads us to discover it.
conn: Manna and the land.
Joshua 5:12: the manna ceased when Israel ate the produce of the land; Jesus is the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–33).
The Exodus.
Exodus 12: God's people go out from slavery; the Spirit leads us from the slavery of the flesh to freedom (Galatians 5:16–18).
The Bereans.
Acts 17:11: they examined the Scriptures daily; the good soil is a heart that studies the Word.
Filled with the spirit.
Micah 3:8: the prophet filled with the spirit of the Lord to speak truth.
altar: “The bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” In the Holy Qurbono we receive the bread that endures for eternal life, and the Spirit makes us bear fruit.
outline: Opening
After Pentecost: what fruit?
Point 1 · The fruit of the Spirit
Love, joy, peace… a portrait of Christ in us.
Point 2 · Good soil
The sower: hearing, holding fast, patient endurance.
Point 3 · Bread that endures
Work for the food of eternal life.
Point 4 · A future with hope
Vocation Day: God's plan for each life.
Take-home line
“If we live by the Spirit, let us also be guided by the Spirit.”
live: Choose one fruit
Pick one fruit of the Spirit (patience, kindness…) to practise deliberately this week.
Read the Word daily (Acts 17:11)
Like the Bereans, read a short passage of Scripture each day.
Pray for vocations
Pray for young people discerning priesthood, religious life or marriage.
fathers: St Augustine
Be good soil: do not let the Word fall on the path of a careless heart, on the rock of a hard heart, or among the thorns of worldly cares (Sermon 73).
St John Chrysostom
The fruit of the Spirit is not something we produce alone; the Spirit works in us, but we must cooperate, as soil receives rain and bears grain (Commentary on Galatians 5).
magis: Catechism 1832
The fruits of the Spirit are perfections that the Holy Spirit forms in us as the first fruits of eternal glory.
Catechism 2707–2708
Meditation on the Word; the parable of the sower.
Catechism 1533–1535
Vocations to marriage and the ordained ministry at the service of communion.
saints: 26 May: St Philip Neri. Weekdays of the season of Pentecost.
2027-05-23.prayer: Holy Spirit, sower of the Word, make our hearts good soil. Bear in us the fruit of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control; feed us with the bread from heaven, and show each of us the plan you have for our lives. Amen.

2027-05-30.title: Second Sunday after Pentecost
readings: You shall be holy, for I am holy
David becomes king over all Israel
The exiles weep, fast and pray
The living God, whose kingdom shall never be destroyed
I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh
No condemnation for those in Christ Jesus
Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it
2027-05-30.verse: Whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
theo: On the morning of Pentecost Peter stands up and explains what the crowds are seeing: it is the fulfilment of Joel: “In the last days it will be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy… Then everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.” The Spirit is not reserved to a few; he is poured out on young and old, men and women, all who call on the Lord.

St Paul tells us what this means for daily life: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and of death… If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies also through his Spirit that dwells in you.” The Spirit who raised Jesus lives in us.

In the evening Gospel Jesus spends the night in prayer on the mountain, then chooses the Twelve and proclaims: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” The Beatitudes are the portrait of a life led by the Spirit, often hidden, often poor, always blessed.

Leviticus gives the deepest command: “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.” Jesus shows the way: “Whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me… whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple… none of these will lose their reward.” Holiness is the Cross carried with love, and the small cup of water given in Christ's name.
conn: Holiness.
Leviticus 19:2: “You shall be holy”; the Spirit is the Holy Spirit, who makes us holy (Romans 8:9–11).
David the king.
2 Samuel 5: the shepherd-king; Jesus, Son of David, chooses the Twelve as shepherds for the new Israel (Luke 6:13).
Daniel's God.
Daniel 6:26: the living God whose kingdom shall never be destroyed; the kingdom Jesus promises to the poor.
Exiles who pray.
Baruch 1:5: the exiles weep, fast and pray; “blessed are you who weep now.”
altar: Jesus prayed all night before choosing the Twelve. Every Holy Qurbono is offered by the Church built on the apostles; the Spirit who raised Jesus gives life to us through the Body and Blood of the Lord.
outline: Opening
After Pentecost: the Spirit for all flesh.
Point 1 · No condemnation
The Spirit of life sets us free.
Point 2 · Blessed are the poor
The Beatitudes as the life of the Spirit.
Point 3 · Be holy
Leviticus 19:2 and our daily choices.
Point 4 · The cross and the cup of water
Great sacrifices and small kindnesses.
Take-home line
“You shall be holy, for I am holy.”
live: A cup of cold water
Do one small, hidden act of kindness each day this week in Jesus' name.
Pray before decisions
Like Jesus before choosing the Twelve, pray before an important decision.
Call on the Lord
Repeat during the day: “Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
fathers: St Ambrose
Luke places poverty first among the beatitudes, for it is the mother of the virtues; whoever despises the world's goods is ready to receive the kingdom (Exposition of Luke 5, 50–53).
St Augustine
The law of the Spirit of life is love poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (On the Spirit and the Letter 17, 29).
magis: Catechism 1716–1717
The Beatitudes depict the countenance of Jesus Christ and portray his charity.
Catechism 2012–2013
All Christians are called to holiness and the perfection of charity.
Lumen Gentium 40
The Lord Jesus preached holiness of life to each and every one of his disciples.
saints: Weekdays of the season of Pentecost. Sunday 6 June: III Sunday after Pentecost.
2027-05-30.prayer: Spirit of life, poured out on all flesh, set us free from sin and death and make us holy as the Father is holy. Teach us the joy of the Beatitudes, give us strength to carry the cross, and let no cup of water given in Christ's name be forgotten. Amen.

2027-05-01.title: Mar Yauseph, Patron of Workers · Jeremiah the Prophet · Saturday of the fourth week after Qyomtho
readings: We worked night and day; anyone unwilling to work should not eat
“Is not this the carpenter’s son?”; a prophet without honour in his own country
2027-05-01.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Mar Yauseph (St Joseph), Patron of Workers, and of Jeremiah the Prophet. 1 May is also May Day, Labour Day in India.
2027-05-01.verse: Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?
theo: On the first of May the whole country remembers its workers. Offices close, unions march, and the radio plays songs about the farmer and the mill hand. On the same morning our Church turns to a workman of Nazareth: the Panchangam keeps the memory of Mar Yauseph, Patron of Workers. Pope Pius XII placed the feast of St Joseph the Worker on 1 May in 1955, so that the day of labour would not belong only to slogans but also to a saint who worked with his hands for the Son of God. The Gospel lets us hear what the neighbours said about that family. When Jesus came home and taught in the synagogue, the people “were astounded and said, ‘Where did this man get this wisdom and these deeds of power? Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?’” They meant it as a put-down. They knew the workshop, the tools and the plain house; how could wisdom come from there? But the Church hears the same words as a title of honour. The eternal Son chose to be known in his own town as the son of a carpenter. Most of his life on earth was spent not in preaching but in work, under the eye of a just man who taught him a trade. Mar Yauseph never speaks a word in the Gospels. His holiness was done with his hands: a door fitted true, a plough beam shaped well, a fair price, a day's labour offered to God.

St Paul writes to the Thessalonians as a fellow worker. Some in that church had stopped working, perhaps thinking the Lord's return was so close that daily labour no longer mattered. Paul reminds them how he lived among them: “we were not idle when we were with you, and we did not eat anyone’s bread without paying for it; but with toil and labor we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you.” He gives them a rule they could not forget: “Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.” And to those who were “living in idleness, mere busybodies, not doing any work,” he says: “do their work quietly and to earn their own living.” This is not harshness towards the poor or the sick or those who cannot find work; the same Paul organised a collection for the hungry church in Jerusalem. It is a word against idleness, which St Benedict called the enemy of the soul (Rule 48, in substance). Work is part of our dignity. In the beginning God put the man in the garden “to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), before there was any sin. The Catechism says that work honours the Creator's gifts and that, borne in union with Jesus, the carpenter of Nazareth and the one crucified on Calvary, it can become a way of holiness (CCC 2427).

The Panchangam also remembers today Jeremiah the Prophet, whom our tradition calls Yeremiah Nbiya. His life matches the Gospel's last line: “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house.” Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, near Jerusalem, called as a young man: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). He spoke for some forty years, and his own townspeople plotted against him; he was beaten, put in the stocks and lowered into a muddy cistern. He wanted to stop, but could not: “within me there is something like a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9). God sent him to a potter's house and showed him the clay being reworked on the wheel: “Just like the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel” (Jeremiah 18:6). A workman's bench became a prophet's pulpit. And it was Jeremiah who foretold the new covenant, God's law written on the heart (31:33), which we shall hear again at Suloko on Thursday. Joseph at his bench, Jeremiah at the potter's wheel, Jesus in the carpenter's house: on Labour Day the Church reminds us that ordinary work, done faithfully, is where God shapes us. Pray today for all workers, for the unemployed and for those who are underpaid or unsafe at work, and offer your own day's work at the Holy Qurbono or in your morning prayer.
conn: The carpenter's son.
Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3: Jesus is called the carpenter's son and the carpenter; the eternal Word learned a trade in the house of Mar Yauseph.
Work from the beginning.
Genesis 2:15 and 2 Thessalonians 3:10: God gave the man the garden to till and keep before the fall; Paul makes honest work the rule of Christian life.
The prophet and the potter.
Jeremiah 18:1–6 and Matthew 13:57: Jeremiah learned God's word at a potter's wheel and was rejected by his own town, as Jesus was at Nazareth.
fathers: St Benedict
Idleness is the enemy of the soul; therefore the brothers should be occupied at fixed times in manual labour, and at fixed hours in holy reading (Rule 48, in substance).
St John Chrysostom

The people of Nazareth should have marvelled all the more that such wisdom came from a humble home; instead they took offence at what ought to have led them to faith (Homilies on Matthew 48, in substance).
magis: Catechism 2427

Human work proceeds directly from persons created in the image of God and called to prolong the work of creation; by enduring the hardship of work in union with Jesus, the carpenter of Nazareth and the one crucified on Calvary, we collaborate with the Son of God in his redemptive work.
Laborem Exercens 6
The one who, while being God, became like us in all things devoted most of the years of his life on earth to manual work at the carpenter's bench.
Redemptoris Custos 22
Work was the daily expression of love in the life of the Family of Nazareth; St Joseph brought human work closer to the mystery of the Redemption.
outline: Opening
Ask: what does my work say about me, and what does it say to God?
Point 1 · The carpenter's son
The Son of God hidden in a workshop with Mar Yauseph.
Point 2 · Work quietly and earn your living
Paul's rule against idleness and the dignity of labour.
Point 3 · The prophet and the potter
Jeremiah, rejected at home and shaped like clay in God's hand.
Take-home line
“Is not this the carpenter’s son?”
live: Offer the day's work (Colossians 3:23)
Before you begin work today, say: “Lord, this is for you,” and do one task with special care.
Pray for workers (2 Thessalonians 3:12)
Pray by name for someone who is looking for work or who is treated unjustly at work, and help them if you can.
2027-05-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you were known in Nazareth as the carpenter's son and learned to work with the hands of Mar Yauseph. By his prayers bless the work of our hands and the labour of every worker; give work to those who seek it, justice to those who are underpaid, safety to those in danger, and rest to the weary. Keep us from idleness and from greed, and like your prophet Jeremiah let us be clay in the Father's hands, shaped by your word. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar we offer bread, the fruit of the earth and the work of human hands; in the Holy Qurbono the risen Lord takes our labour into his own offering and gives us himself.

2027-05-03.title: Monday of the fifth week after Qyomtho
readings: Now is the acceptable time; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything
“I am the light of the world”
2027-05-03.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fifth Sunday after Qyomtho; Suloko, the Ascension of our Lord, is on Thursday 6 May.
2027-05-03.verse: See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!
theo: Three days before Suloko the readings speak of time and of light. St Paul begins with an appeal: “As we work together with him, we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain.” Then he quotes the prophet Isaiah, “At an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you,” and turns the old promise into a present fact: “See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” We are always tempted to place God's time somewhere else: in the past, when we were more fervent, or in the future, when the children are settled, the loan is paid and life is quieter. Paul says no. The day of salvation is today, this Monday morning, with the work and the worries it brings. The Risen Lord does not wait for better circumstances to meet us. In these last days of the fifty days of Qyomtho the Church is preparing to see him ascend and to receive his Spirit; the preparation happens now or it does not happen at all.

Then Paul draws a portrait of the apostolic life, and it is not what anyone would choose. He lists “great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger.” Alongside these he names the weapons of a servant of God: “purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, holiness of spirit, genuine love, truthful speech, and the power of God.” And he ends with a chain of paradoxes that only Easter can explain: “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.” How can someone who has nothing possess everything? Only if the one thing he has is Christ, in whom all things hold together. St John Chrysostom, commenting on this passage, said that Paul lists the hardships not to boast but to show that the grace of God was strong enough to carry him through them all (Homilies on 2 Corinthians 12, in substance). The Christian is not someone protected from trouble; he is someone in whom joy survives trouble.

In the Gospel Jesus says in the temple: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.” He spoke these words, John notes, “in the treasury of the temple,” close to where the great lamps were lit at the feast of Tabernacles. The Pharisees object that he is testifying for himself, and Jesus answers that he does not stand alone: “I testify on my own behalf, and the Father who sent me testifies on my behalf.” The argument is a reminder that faith is not a private opinion; it rests on the witness of the Father to the Son, and soon, at Pentecost, on the witness of the Spirit. Our Church begins each day with the morning prayer of the Shehimo, greeting Christ as the light that has dawned on us. Let the light be practical today: switch off one thing that darkens your mind, open one page of the Gospel, and walk in the light by one honest act. “No one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.” His hour came on the Cross, and its light still shines from the empty tomb.
outline: Opening
Ask: am I waiting for a better time to give myself to God?
Point 1 · Now is the day of salvation
Grace is not to be received in vain; God's time is today.
Point 2 · Having nothing, possessing everything
Paul's paradoxes and the joy that survives trouble.
Point 3 · The light of the world
Following Jesus out of darkness, with the Father's witness.
Take-home line
“See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!”
live: Do it today (2 Corinthians 6:2)
Name one good thing you have been postponing for God, a confession, a visit, a reconciliation, and do it before the week ends.
Walk in the light (John 8:12)
Turn off one source of darkness in your evening, and read John 8:12 before you sleep.
2027-05-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you are the light of the world, and whoever follows you will not walk in darkness. Do not let us receive your grace in vain. Teach us that now is the acceptable time and today the day of salvation. When we are sorrowful, keep us rejoicing; when we are poor, make us rich in you; when we have nothing, let us possess everything by possessing you. Prepare our hearts to see you ascend and to receive your Holy Spirit. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the light of the world comes to us under the humble signs of bread and wine; having nothing in ourselves, we receive everything in him.

2027-05-04.title: Tuesday of the fifth week after Qyomtho
readings: Gentle like a nurse; sharing not only the gospel but our own selves
“Whoever keeps my word will never see death”
2027-05-04.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fifth Sunday after Qyomtho; Suloko, the Ascension of our Lord, is on Thursday 6 May.
2027-05-04.verse: So deeply do we care for you that we are determined to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you have become very dear to us.
theo: Thessalonica was one of Paul's shortest missions. He had arrived there bruised from Philippi, preached for a few weeks, and was forced to leave by night. Now, writing back to the young church, he remembers how he had lived among them, and the letter becomes a portrait of a pastor's heart. “You yourselves know, brothers and sisters, that our coming to you was not in vain, but though we had already suffered and been shamefully mistreated at Philippi, as you know, we had courage in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in spite of great opposition.” The courage did not come from Paul's temperament; it came “in our God.” And his motive was clean: “we speak, not to please mortals, but to please God who tests our hearts.” He had not used flattery, had not looked for money, had not sought praise. Every preacher, every catechism teacher, every parent who speaks of God at home can examine himself by these lines. Am I trying to be liked, or trying to be faithful? God tests the heart, and the heart is where the Gospel either rings true or sounds hollow.

Then Paul uses two images that are surprising from a man so often pictured as stern. “But we were gentle among you, like a nurse tenderly caring for her own children.” And a few lines later: “we dealt with each one of you like a father with his children, urging and encouraging you and pleading that you lead a life worthy of God.” Mother and father together: tenderness and firmness, care and challenge. At the centre is the verse that sums up all ministry: “So deeply do we care for you that we are determined to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you have become very dear to us.” A message alone is not enough. The Gospel travels from person to person through shared lives, through time given, meals eaten together, nights of work so as not to be a burden. Paul again mentions his manual labour: “we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.” St Gregory the Great wrote that the pastor must be near to each one in compassion and raised above all in contemplation, so that he can carry the weaknesses of others in his own heart (Pastoral Rule II.5, in substance).

In the Gospel the argument in the temple grows sharp. Some of Jesus' hearers say, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” When John speaks of “the Jews” in passages like this he means those among the leaders and hearers who opposed Jesus in that hour, not the Jewish people as a whole, of whom Jesus himself, his Mother and all the apostles were members; the Church firmly rejects any blame of the Jewish people for these quarrels (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Jesus does not answer insult with insult. He says simply, “I do not have a demon; but I honor my Father,” and then he makes one of the great promises of the fourth Gospel: “Very truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.” In the season of Qyomtho we hear it with Easter ears. The one who says it has already passed through death and come out the other side. To keep his word is to be joined to his risen life, so that bodily death, when it comes, is no longer the end but a door. Keeping his word begins in small things: the word of forgiveness I must speak, the word of truth I must not bend. Like Paul at Thessalonica, we keep it best when we share it with our whole life.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I speak of God, am I trying to please people or God?
Point 1 · To please God who tests our hearts
Courage in God, and a clean motive.
Point 2 · Gentle like a nurse, firm like a father
Sharing the Gospel and our own selves.
Point 3 · Whoever keeps my word
The risen Lord's promise against death.
Take-home line
“Not only the gospel of God but also our own selves.”
live: Share yourself (1 Thessalonians 2:8)
Give someone in your family or parish an unhurried hour this week: a visit, a meal, a long listening.
Keep one word (John 8:51)
Choose one saying of Jesus from this week's readings and live it deliberately for a whole day.
2027-05-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you promised that whoever keeps your word will never see death. Give us courage in God to speak your Gospel, and purity of heart to seek only to please the Father who tests our hearts. Make our priests, teachers and parents gentle as a nurse and firm as a father, ready to share not only your word but their own selves. Keep us in your word, that we may share your risen life for ever. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar Christ does what Paul could only imitate: he shares with us not only his word but his own self, his Body and Blood, in the Holy Qurbono.

2027-05-05.title: Wednesday of the fifth week after Qyomtho
readings: Pray for us; the Lord is faithful and will guard you from the evil one
Your eye is the lamp of your body
2027-05-05.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fifth Sunday after Qyomtho; Suloko, the Ascension of our Lord, is on Thursday 6 May. Tomorrow is Suloko: prepare to take part in the Holy Qurbono.
2027-05-05.verse: But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
theo: On the eve of Suloko St Paul asks his people for something he could not do without: “Finally, brothers and sisters, pray for us, so that the word of the Lord may spread rapidly and be glorified everywhere, just as it is among you, and that we may be rescued from wicked and evil people; for not all have faith.” The great apostle does not stand above the community; he leans on its prayer. The Greek picture behind “spread rapidly” is of a runner: Paul wants the word of the Lord to run through the world. Tomorrow Jesus will be lifted up from his disciples and will send them, in St Mark's words, to “go into all the world and proclaim the good news.” The mission belongs to the whole Church, and the first way each of us shares in it is by prayer for those who preach. Pray this week for your bishop and your parish priest by name, for missionaries in the north of India and abroad, for catechism teachers preparing children for First Holy Qurbono. Paul knew that the word does not spread by human cleverness. It runs when the Church prays.

Then Paul turns from his own needs to the faithfulness of God: “But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.” People may fail, not all have faith, but the Lord does not fail. The phrase “the evil one” is the same as in the Lord's Prayer, which our Church prays many times each day, when we ask to be delivered from the evil one. Paul ends with a blessing worth learning by heart: “May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.” The word for direct means to straighten a path, to clear the road ahead. Love of God and the steadfastness, the patient endurance, of Christ are the two rails on which the Christian life runs. St Augustine wrote that our hearts are directed to the love of God when we love God for his own sake and everything else for his sake (in substance, after his teaching on the order of love in On Christian Doctrine I). The Lord who is faithful will do the straightening, if we let him.

The Gospel speaks of light and of seeing. “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar, but on the lampstand so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. If your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light.” In Kerala homes the nilavilakku is lit at dusk and set where all can see it; no one hides it under a cot. Jesus says the eye works like that lamp: what we look at, and how we look, fills us either with light or with darkness. “Therefore consider whether the light in you is not darkness.” A sobering question for an age of screens. On the eve of the Ascension, when the disciples will stand gazing up into heaven, Jesus asks us to look with a clear eye: at God, at our neighbour, at the world, without greed or envy or impurity. Tomorrow, at Suloko, the Church will lift its eyes to the ascending Lord. Prepare tonight with a short examination of what your eyes have taken in today, and ask for a healthy eye, so that your whole life may become a lamp on the stand.
outline: Opening
Ask: who is praying for me, and for whom do I pray?
Point 1 · Pray for us
That the word of the Lord may run through the world.
Point 2 · The Lord is faithful
Strength and protection from the evil one; hearts directed to love and steadfastness.
Point 3 · Your eye is the lamp of your body
A clear eye and a lamp on the stand, on the eve of Suloko.
Take-home line
“But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.”
live: Pray for those who preach (2 Thessalonians 3:1)
Pray each day this week, by name, for your bishop, your parish priest and one missionary you know.
Guard your eyes (Luke 11:34)
Tonight, before you sleep, recall what your eyes looked at today, and turn away tomorrow from one thing that darkens you.
2027-05-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, tomorrow we celebrate your going up to the Father. Let your word run through the world and be glorified, and strengthen all who proclaim it. You are faithful: strengthen us and guard us from the evil one. Direct our hearts to the love of God and to your own steadfastness. Make our eyes healthy and our lives full of light, so that we may be lamps on the stand for all who enter your house. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the Church lifts up its eyes and its heart to the Lord; the faithful one who strengthens us gives himself as food for the journey of mission.

2027-05-07.title: The Finding of the Cross of our Lord · First Friday · Friday after Suloko
readings: May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ
The treasure hidden in a field; the pearl of great value
2027-05-07.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), after Suloko (the Ascension): the ten days of waiting and prayer for the Holy Spirit before Pentecost. The Panchangam notes that weddings are not celebrated in these days. The Panchangam keeps today the Finding of the Cross of our Lord. It is also the First Friday of May.
2027-05-07.verse: May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
theo: Yesterday the Church watched the Lord go up into heaven. Today, on the first day of the ten days of waiting, the Panchangam turns our eyes back to the wood on which he died: it keeps the Finding of the Cross of our Lord. This is not a step backwards. The one who ascended is the Crucified; he carries the marks of the nails into the glory of the Father, and the Cross is the road by which he went up. Our Malankara tradition calls the Cross the Sleeba, and we never pray without it: we sign ourselves at the beginning and the end of every prayer, the priest blesses with the hand cross, and the bare cross on our altars, without a figure, proclaims that the Crucified is risen. What can be said with confidence about the finding is this. In the reign of the emperor Constantine, the place of Golgotha and the tomb had been uncovered in Jerusalem and a great church built over them. St Cyril of Jerusalem, preaching there around 350, could already say that the wood of the Cross had been distributed in fragments over the whole world (Catechetical Lectures 4.10; 13.4, in substance). By the end of that century St Ambrose of Milan told how St Helena, Constantine's mother, had searched Golgotha and found the Cross (On the Death of Theodosius 43–46, in substance). The details belong to tradition; the heart of the feast is certain. The Cross is not lost. It was found, and it is found again whenever a Christian chooses it.

St Paul ends his letter to the Galatians in his own handwriting: “See what large letters I make when I am writing in my own hand!” He has argued at length with those who wanted the Gentile converts to be circumcised, and now he gathers everything into one sentence: “May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” To boast is to rest your worth on something. People boast of family, money, education, the size of their house or their church. Paul rests his whole worth on the Cross, where the Son of God “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Then he adds: “For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything; but a new creation is everything!” The Cross makes new creatures. And he closes with a line that only a man who had been beaten and stoned could write: “I carry the marks of Jesus branded on my body.” St John Chrysostom, commenting here, said that what seems a reproach to the world is for Paul the cause of countless blessings, and so he glories in it (Commentary on Galatians 6, in substance). The Cross is the place where the world's values are turned upside down: weakness becomes strength, shame becomes glory, death becomes life.

The Gospel gives the feast its picture. “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which someone found and hid; then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.” The finder does not sell everything grudgingly; he does it “in his joy.” So it is with the Cross. To the world it looks like loss; to the one who has found it, it is the treasure that makes everything else worth selling. The merchant who finds “one pearl of great value” does the same. On this First Friday many of our parishes keep the devotion to the Sacred Heart: the Heart of Jesus opened on the Cross, from which “at once blood and water came out” (John 19:34), the Church's sacraments of Baptism and the Holy Qurbono. The Catechism says that the Heart of Jesus, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is the sign and symbol of the love with which he loves us (CCC 478). Make the sign of the Cross today slowly and with attention. Go to confession if you can, and take part in the Holy Qurbono. And in these ten days, as we wait for the Spirit, ask for the grace to boast of nothing but the Cross, and to find in it the hidden treasure of your life.
conn: The serpent lifted up.
Numbers 21:8–9 and John 3:14–15: the bronze serpent on the pole, which healed those who looked at it, foreshadowed the Son of Man lifted up on the Cross.
The treasure found.
Matthew 13:44 and Philippians 3:8: Paul counted everything as loss for the surpassing value of knowing Christ crucified and risen.
The pierced Heart.
Zechariah 12:10 and John 19:34–37: they shall look on the one whom they have pierced; from his opened side came blood and water.
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem

Let us not be ashamed of the Cross of Christ; even if others hide it, seal it openly on your forehead, so that the demons may see the royal sign and flee trembling far away (Catechetical Lectures 13.36, in substance).
St John Chrysostom

What seems a reproach to the world is to Paul the cause of countless blessings; therefore he glories in the Cross, by which he died to the world and the world to him (Commentary on Galatians 6, in substance).
magis: Catechism 618
The Cross is the unique sacrifice of Christ, the one mediator between God and men; he calls his disciples to take up their cross and follow him, for Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example.
Catechism 478
Jesus knew and loved us each and all during his life, his agony and his Passion; the Sacred Heart of Jesus, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is the sign and symbol of that love.
Catechism 2157
The Christian begins his day, his prayers and his activities with the sign of the Cross, dedicating the day to the glory of God.
outline: Opening
Ask: what do I boast of, what do I rest my worth on?
Point 1 · Boasting only in the Cross
Paul's own handwriting, the new creation, and the marks of Jesus.
Point 2 · A treasure hidden in a field
The Cross found in Jerusalem and found again in every heart that chooses it.
Point 3 · The pierced Heart
First Friday: blood and water from the opened side.
Take-home line
“May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
live: The sign of the Cross (Galatians 6:14)
Make the sign of the Cross slowly and attentively each time you begin and end a prayer today.
First Friday (John 19:34)
Go to confession if you can, take part in the Holy Qurbono, or spend some minutes before the Blessed Sacrament for the Heart of Jesus.
2027-05-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen and ascended, you carried the marks of your Cross into the glory of the Father. On this day of the Finding of your Cross we thank you for the holy wood on which you redeemed the world. Let us boast of nothing but your Cross; crucify the world to us and us to the world, and make us a new creation. Show us the hidden treasure and give us the joy to sell all for it. From your pierced Heart pour out on us the blood and water of your mercy, and as we wait for the Holy Spirit, keep us under the sign of the Cross. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The sacrifice of the Cross is made present on our altar in the Holy Qurbono; the bare cross above it tells us that the Crucified is risen and feeds us with his Body and Blood.

2027-05-08.title: Mar Yohannan Shleeha · St John the Apostle · Saturday after Suloko
readings: Who will separate us from the love of Christ?
The disciple whom Jesus loved; “Follow me!”
2027-05-08.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), after Suloko (the Ascension): the ten days of waiting and prayer for the Holy Spirit before Pentecost. The Panchangam notes that weddings are not celebrated in these days. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Mar Yohannan Shleeha, St John the Apostle, and the founding of the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary (1938).
2027-05-08.verse: This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and we know that his testimony is true.
theo: Today the Panchangam remembers Mar Yohannan Shleeha, St John the Apostle, son of Zebedee and brother of Mar Yaqob, whom the Panchangam remembered on 30 April. He was a fisherman of Galilee, called with his brother from their father's boat; with Peter and James he saw the raising of Jairus' daughter, the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane. The Church's tradition, from St Irenaeus of Lyons in the second century, recognises him as “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” who leaned on the Lord's breast at the Supper and later gave the Church the fourth Gospel while living at Ephesus (Against Heresies III.1.1, in substance). Many Eastern Churches keep his memory on this day in May. The Gospel shows him in the last scene by the lake after the Resurrection. Jesus has just asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and told him to feed his sheep. Then “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them.” Peter asks, “Lord, what about him?” and Jesus answers, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me!” Each disciple has his own road. Peter will glorify God by a martyr's death; John will remain long, bearing witness. We are not to measure our call against another's. The only question that matters is the one Jesus puts to each of us: will you follow me?

The Gospel ends with John's own seal: “This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and we know that his testimony is true.” The beloved disciple is above all a witness. He stood at the Cross when others had fled, he ran to the empty tomb and “saw and believed,” and he recognised the risen Lord on the shore before anyone else: “It is the Lord!” Love made him see. St Paul's words in the Epistle could stand over John's whole life: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will hardship, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” And the answer: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” Nothing in all creation, “neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come,” can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. St Jerome tells that when John was very old at Ephesus and could no longer walk, he was carried into the assembly and would say only, “Little children, love one another.” When asked why he always repeated it, he answered that it was the Lord's command, and if this alone were done, it would be enough (Commentary on Galatians 6:10, in substance). The apostle of love ended as he began, resting on the heart of Christ.

From the Cross Jesus entrusted his Mother to this disciple: “Here is your mother,” and “from that hour the disciple took her into his own home” (John 19:27). It is fitting, then, that today the Panchangam also remembers the founding of the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, the Mary Makkal, on 8 May 1938 at Marthandam, in the time of the Servant of God Archbishop Mar Ivanios. Like John, the sisters took the Mother of the Lord into their home and their name. For nearly ninety years they have gone to the villages and to the poor in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and far beyond, in mission, teaching, nursing and the care of the forgotten, bearing quiet witness that nothing can separate us from the love of Christ. Thank God today for the sisters you know, pray for vocations to religious life in our Church, and ask Mar Yohannan to teach you his two lessons: to rest on the heart of Christ in prayer, and to take Mary, the Mother of God, into your home. As we wait in these days for the Holy Spirit, we wait as the apostles did, “constantly devoting themselves to prayer” with Mary the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14).
conn: The beloved disciple.
John 13:23 and 21:20: the disciple who reclined next to Jesus at the Supper follows Jesus after the Resurrection; the Church's tradition knows him as John.
The Mother entrusted.
John 19:26–27 and Acts 1:14: John took Mary into his home; the apostles waited for the Spirit in prayer with her.
Love stronger than death.
Song of Songs 8:6 and Romans 8:38–39: love is strong as death; nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ.
fathers: St Irenaeus of Lyons
John, the disciple of the Lord, who also leaned upon his breast, himself published a Gospel while living at Ephesus in Asia (Against Heresies III.1.1, in substance).
St Jerome

The blessed John, in extreme old age at Ephesus, was carried to the church and said only, “Little children, love one another”; asked why, he replied that this is the Lord's command, and if it alone is done, it is enough (Commentary on Galatians 6:10, in substance).
magis: Catechism 2618, 964
Mary's union with her Son continued to his death, when he gave her as mother to the disciple: “Woman, here is your son.”
Lumen Gentium 58
The Blessed Virgin stood by the Cross and was given by the dying Christ Jesus as a mother to his disciple.
Vita Consecrata 28
In the life of consecrated persons Mary has a special place; she is the example of consecration to the Father and of union with the Son.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is that to you? Follow me! Where am I comparing my road with another's?
Point 1 · The disciple whom Jesus loved
Resting on Christ's heart; a witness whose testimony is true.
Point 2 · Who will separate us?
Paul's hymn of love that nothing can defeat.
Point 3 · He took her into his home
Mary entrusted to John; the Daughters of Mary founded in 1938.
Take-home line
“Who will separate us from the love of Christ?”
live: Little children, love one another (1 John 4:7)
Do one quiet act of love today for someone in your home who is hard to love.
Take Mary into your home (John 19:27)
Pray the Rosary or a Marian prayer together as a family this evening, and pray for the sisters who serve in our Church.
2027-05-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you loved Mar Yohannan Shleeha and let him rest on your heart; from the Cross you gave him your Mother, and after your Resurrection you called him to follow you. By his prayers make us witnesses whose testimony is true, convinced that nothing can separate us from your love. Bless the Daughters of Mary and all consecrated women, and give our Church many generous vocations. Teach us to take your Mother into our homes, and to wait with her in prayer for the Holy Spirit. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The beloved disciple leaned on the Lord's breast at the Supper; in the Holy Qurbono we too come close to the heart of Christ and receive the love from which nothing can separate us.

2027-05-10.title: Mar Shemun Shleeha the Zealot · St Simon the Apostle · Monday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: Paul stays in Ephesus until Pentecost: a wide door for effective work has opened
Zacchaeus: today salvation has come to this house
2027-05-10.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Mar Shemun Shleeha the Zealot, St Simon the Apostle.
2027-05-10.verse: For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.
theo: Four days after Suloko, the Church is in the upper room. The Lord has gone up to the Father, the Spirit has not yet come, and the Panchangam reminds us that in these ten days no wedding celebrations are held: the whole Church holds its breath and prays. It is fitting that today we remember one of the men who sat in that very room. St Luke gives the list of those who waited: “Peter, and John, and James, and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, and Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James.” This is Mar Shemun Shleeha, whom our Church calls “the zealous one.” St Matthew and St Mark call him “the Cananaean,” from an Aramaic word for zeal; St Luke translates it as “the Zealot.” Whether Simon had belonged to the party of armed patriots who longed to drive out the Romans, or whether the name simply marked a man burning with zeal for God's Law, the Gospels do not say, and scholars still discuss it. What happened to him after Pentecost is told differently by different Churches: some ancient traditions send him with St Jude to preach in Persia and to die there as a martyr; others speak of Egypt or other lands. We hold to what is sure: Jesus chose him, Jesus changed the direction of his zeal, and on the day of Pentecost he was among those on whom the fire came down.

The Gospel shows us why such a man could follow Jesus. In Jericho there lived Zacchaeus, “a chief tax collector” who “was rich.” Tax collectors worked for the occupying power and often took more than was due; a zealot would have counted him a traitor to his people. Yet Zacchaeus, short in stature and long in curiosity, “ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see him.” Jesus stopped beneath the tree: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today.” The crowd grumbled, “He has gone to be the guest of one who is a sinner.” But grace had already done its work. Zacchaeus stood and said, “Look, half of my possessions, Lord, I will give to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I will pay back four times as much.” Then came the great word: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.” Think of the company of the Twelve: Simon the Zealot and Matthew the tax collector sat at the same table and ate the same bread. Only Jesus could make brothers of such men. St Augustine says that Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore as we must climb the Cross: the humble wood that seems foolish to the proud is the place from which we see the Lord passing by (Sermon 174, in substance). Simon's zeal did not die when he met Jesus; it was turned from hatred of the sinner to love of the lost.

St Paul's words to the Corinthians come from the same season of the year. “I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,” he writes, “for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” Paul counted the days towards Pentecost, as we do now. He saw a door open, and he saw opposition too, and he did not run from either. Then he speaks with tenderness of his younger helper: “If Timothy comes, see that he has nothing to fear among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord just as I am; therefore let no one despise him.” And of Apollos, who would not come just then: “He will come when he has the opportunity.” Here is zeal that has learned patience and gentleness. It does not crush the young or force the reluctant; it waits for God's time. That is the lesson of these ten days. The apostles did not rush out of the upper room on the day after the Ascension to begin their own campaign. They waited, “constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus.” Holy zeal begins on its knees. Then the Spirit opens the wide door.
conn: The Zealot in the upper room.
Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13: Simon is named among the Twelve and among those who waited in prayer with Mary for the Holy Spirit.
Zeal for the Father's house.
Psalm 69:9, quoted in John 2:17: the zeal that consumed Jesus is the zeal he gives to his apostles, a zeal for God and for the lost.
The lost sought and saved.
Luke 19:10 echoes Ezekiel 34:16, where God promises to seek the lost himself; in Jesus the Shepherd of Israel walks into Jericho.
fathers: St Augustine
Zacchaeus was small and climbed a tree to see Jesus; let us also climb the tree of the Cross, which the proud mock, so that we may see the Lord who passes by (Sermon 174, in substance).
St Ambrose
Let the rich learn that the fault lies not in possessions themselves but in those who do not know how to use them; Zacchaeus became great by giving (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke 8, in substance).
magis: Catechism 858

Jesus is the Father's Emissary. From the beginning of his ministry, he called to him those whom he desired, and appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him and to be sent out to preach.
Catechism 2447

The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbour in his spiritual and bodily necessities; giving alms to the poor is one of the chief witnesses to fraternal charity.
Lumen Gentium 19

The Lord Jesus, after praying to the Father, called to himself those whom he desired and appointed twelve to be with him; he formed them after the manner of a college, and sent them to proclaim the Kingdom of God (in substance).
outline: Opening
Ask: what am I zealous about, and does my zeal look like Jesus?
Point 1 · Simon the Zealot
A burning heart chosen and turned towards the Kingdom.
Point 2 · Today salvation has come
Zacchaeus, the tax collector, found by the Lord who seeks the lost.
Point 3 · A wide door at Pentecost
Zeal that waits, prays and is gentle with others.
Take-home line
“For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.”
live: Hurry and come down (Luke 19:5)
Think of one person you have written off as beyond change. Pray for that person by name every day until Pentecost.
Let no one despise him (1 Corinthians 16:11)
Find one young person in your parish or family who is doing the Lord's work, and give a word of encouragement this week.
2027-05-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came to seek out and to save the lost, and you stopped beneath the sycamore tree to call Zacchaeus by name. You chose Mar Shemun the Zealot and turned the fire of his heart towards your Kingdom. In these days of waiting between your Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit, gather us with your apostles and with your holy Mother in prayer. Purify our zeal from anger and pride, make it patient and gentle, and open for us the wide door of your work. By the prayers of Mar Shemun Shleeha, let salvation come to our homes today, and make us glad to welcome you. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: Zacchaeus received Jesus into his house and was changed; at the Holy Qurbono the Lord says to each of us again, “I must stay at your house today,” and comes to us in his Body and Blood.

2027-05-11.title: Sts Cyril and Methodius of the Slav peoples · Tuesday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: God's plan to gather up all things in Christ; sealed with the promised Holy Spirit
Jesus prays all night on the mountain and chooses the Twelve
2027-05-11.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Sts Cyril and Methodius of the Slav peoples.
2027-05-11.verse: In him you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and had believed in him, were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit
theo: Today the Panchangam names two brothers from far away: Sts Cyril and Methodius, the apostles of the Slav peoples. They were born in Thessalonica in the ninth century, sons of a Greek family who knew the Slavonic speech of the villages around the city. Constantine, the younger, was a scholar so gifted that he was called “the Philosopher”; Methodius, the elder, had been a governor before he became a monk. In 863 the prince of Great Moravia, in the lands of today's Czech Republic and Slovakia, asked the Emperor in Constantinople for teachers who could explain the faith to his people in their own tongue. The brothers were sent. Before they left, Constantine made an alphabet for a language that had never been written, the script now called Glagolitic, and began to translate the Gospels. The first words he wrote, according to the old account of his life, were the opening of St John: “In the beginning was the Word.” Then came the Psalms, the readings and the prayers of the Liturgy, so that the Slavs heard the Holy Mysteries celebrated in words they understood.

Not everyone was pleased. Some clergy held that God should be praised only in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, the three languages written over the Cross. The brothers went to Rome, and Pope Adrian II received them with honour and approved the Slavonic books for the Liturgy. There, in 869, Constantine fell ill; he took the monastic name Cyril and died, still young. Methodius returned as archbishop and laboured for sixteen more years, through opposition and even imprisonment, until he died in 885. The Eastern Churches call them “equal to the apostles,” and in 1980 St John Paul II named them patrons of Europe together with St Benedict. Their memory fits the Gospel of the day. Before choosing the Twelve, Jesus “went out to the mountain to pray; and he spent the night in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles.” Every true mission begins in that night of prayer. The names that follow, Simon Peter and Andrew, James and John, down to Judas Iscariot, show that the Lord chooses real and different people, and that the Church grows from his choice, not from our cleverness. Cyril and Methodius were not among the Twelve, but they carried the same mission to people the Twelve never saw.

St Paul's hymn in Ephesians shows the goal of all mission. God has made known to us “the mystery of his will,” “a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.” Christ does not erase the peoples of the earth; he gathers them, with their languages and songs, into one praise. And the seal of this gathering is the Holy Spirit: “In him you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and had believed in him, were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit; this is the pledge of our inheritance.” In five days we shall keep Pentecost, when the apostles spoke and every listener heard “in our own languages” the mighty works of God. Our own Church knows this gift. The Holy Qurbono that our fathers prayed in Syriac is offered today in Malayalam and in many other tongues, while the ancient Syriac words and melodies remain in it like old gold. What Cyril and Methodius did for the Slavs, the Spirit does in every land: he makes the one Gospel at home in every language, so that every people may say “Abba, Father.”
fathers: The Life of Constantine (Cyril)

Does not the rain fall from God upon all alike, and does not the sun shine on all? Are you not ashamed to recognise only three languages and to command all other peoples and tribes to be blind and deaf? (Life of Constantine 16, in substance).
St Irenaeus of Lyons

The Church, though scattered through the whole world, keeps the faith carefully as if she lived in one house; though the languages of the world differ, the meaning of the tradition is one and the same (Against Heresies 1.10.2, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1204

The celebration of the liturgy should correspond to the genius and culture of the different peoples; in order that the mystery of Christ be made known to all the nations, it must be proclaimed, celebrated and lived in all cultures, which it does not abolish but redeems and fulfils (in substance).
Slavorum Apostoli 9

The two brothers wished to become similar in every aspect to those to whom they were bringing the Gospel; they wished to become part of those peoples and to share their lot in everything (in substance).
Orientalium Ecclesiarum 1

The Catholic Church holds in high esteem the institutions, liturgical rites, ecclesiastical traditions and Christian way of life of the Eastern Churches, in which shines forth the tradition handed down from the apostles through the Fathers (in substance).
outline: Opening
Ask: in what language does my heart pray when no one is listening?
Point 1 · A night of prayer before the choosing
Jesus prays, then names the Twelve.
Point 2 · All things gathered in Christ
Two brothers who gave the Slavs the Gospel in their own tongue.
Point 3 · Sealed with the Spirit
The pledge of our inheritance, and Pentecost five days away.
Take-home line
“Marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit.”
live: He spent the night in prayer (Luke 6:12)
Before a big decision this month, give one evening hour to prayer before you choose.
To gather up all things in him (Ephesians 1:10)
Learn one prayer or hymn of our Church by heart this week, and teach it to a child in the family.
2027-05-11.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, before you chose your apostles you spent the night in prayer to the Father, and you sent them to gather all peoples into your Kingdom. We thank you for Sts Cyril and Methodius, who gave the Slav peoples your Gospel and your holy Mysteries in their own tongue. In these days of waiting for the Holy Spirit, seal us again with the promised Spirit, the pledge of our inheritance. Make our homes and our parish places where your word is heard and understood, and let every language on earth sing the praise of your glory. Through the prayers of your holy Mother and of all your saints, gather up all things in yourself. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Spirit is called down upon the bread and wine, and upon us; the one Body of Christ is offered in every tongue, and all who receive it are gathered into one.

2027-05-12.title: Mar Epiphanios of Cyprus · Mar Yaqob, bishop and Malpan of Nisibis · Wednesday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: Work out your salvation, for God is at work in you; shine like stars in the world
