Interpret the present time; settle with your accuser on the way
2027-05-12.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Mar Epiphanios of Cyprus and of Mar Yaqob, bishop and Malpan of Nisibis (St Jacob of Nisibis).
2027-05-12.verse: for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
theo: The Panchangam joins two bishops of the fourth century today, one from the Greek world and one from the Syriac. Mar Yaqob of Nisibis was the first bishop of that frontier city between the Roman and Persian empires, in the south-east of today's Turkey. He sat among the bishops of the Council of Nicaea in 325, where the Church confessed that the Son is “of one being with the Father.” Our Church calls him Malpan, teacher, and Syriac tradition remembers him as the teacher of St Ephrem, who grew up in Nisibis and sang its bishops in his hymns. Theodoret of Cyrrhus tells that when the Persian king laid siege to the city, the bishop's prayers were its true wall (Religious History 1); whatever the details of that story, the people of Nisibis never forgot a shepherd who stood with them in danger. Mar Epiphanios was born in Palestine, became a monk, and in 367 was chosen bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, where he served for more than thirty-five years. He was a man of vast learning and fierce zeal for the true faith. His great book, the Panarion, or “medicine chest,” gathered the errors of his time and set beside each one the remedy of the apostolic faith. Among those he answered were some who denied that the Mother of God remained a virgin, and others who offered sacrifice to her as to a goddess. To both he gave the Church's balanced answer: “Let Mary be held in honour, but let the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be worshipped; let no one worship Mary” (Panarion 79.7, in substance). Honour for the Mother, worship for God alone: that is still our faith.

St Paul's words to the Philippians describe the life of such shepherds and of every believer. “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.” There is no contest here between God's grace and our effort. God works, and therefore we work; his grace gives both the desire and the strength. Then Paul asks for a certain kind of life: “Do all things without murmuring and arguing, so that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine like stars in the world.” A star does not argue with the darkness; it simply shines. And Paul adds a line that sounds like the voice of a martyr: “even if I am being poured out as a libation over the sacrifice and the offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you.” The bishops we remember today poured out their lives in that way, in study, in teaching, in the defence of their people.

The Gospel brings us back to these days of waiting. Jesus says to the crowds: “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you immediately say, ‘It is going to rain’; and so it happens... You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?” In Kerala we know the signs of the monsoon well; in mid-May every farmer watches the western sky. The Church watches too. The Lord has ascended; the promised Spirit is near. This is a present time to be read rightly. And Jesus says what a wise person does when trouble is coming: “when you go with your accuser before a magistrate, on the way make an effort to settle the case.” We are all on the way. Before the day of the Lord, before Pentecost, before the next Holy Qurbono, there may be someone with whom we must make peace. Jesus asks us to settle it now, on the road, while there is still time. The Spirit comes most fully into hearts that have forgiven.
fathers: St Epiphanius of Salamis

Let Mary be held in honour, but let the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be worshipped; let no one worship Mary. The mystery is due to God, not to a woman, not even to a man (Panarion 79.7, in substance).
St Ephrem the Syrian

In his hymns for Nisibis, Ephrem praises the first shepherds of the city, beginning with Jacob, as fathers who guarded the flock through hard years and handed on the faith unbroken (Hymns on Nisibis 13–16, in substance).
magis: Lumen Gentium 66

Mary is rightly honoured by a special cult in the Church; this cult, as it always existed, differs essentially from the cult of adoration which is offered to the Incarnate Word, as well as to the Father and the Holy Spirit, and it fosters that adoration (in substance).
Catechism 2001

The preparation of man for the reception of grace is already a work of grace; God brings to completion in us what he has begun, for he begins by working so that we may will, and completes by cooperating with our will.
Catechism 2840
The outpouring of God's mercy cannot penetrate our hearts as long as we have not forgiven those who have trespassed against us.
outline: Opening
Ask: what sign is God giving me in this present time, and am I reading it?
Point 1 · God at work in you
Grace gives both the will and the work.
Point 2 · Shining like stars
Two bishops who poured out their lives for the true faith.
Point 3 · Settle it on the way
Reading the present time and making peace before the Spirit comes.
Take-home line
“It is God who is at work in you.”
live: Without murmuring and arguing (Philippians 2:14)
For three days, keep a guard on your tongue: no complaining at home or at work. Offer each held-back complaint as a prayer.
Make an effort to settle the case (Luke 12:58)
Before Pentecost, take one step towards peace with someone you are at odds with: a call, a visit, a message.
2027-05-12.prayer: Lord God, you are at work in us, giving us both the will and the strength to do your good pleasure. We thank you for Mar Yaqob of Nisibis and Mar Epiphanios of Cyprus, shepherds who guarded the faith of Nicaea and poured out their lives for your people. Teach us to honour the Mother of your Son as they did, and to worship you alone, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Help us to read the signs of this present time, and to make peace on the way with all whom we have wronged, so that our hearts may be ready for the coming of your Spirit. Make us shine like stars in the world, holding fast to the word of life. Through Christ our Lord, to whom with you and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: St Paul speaks of being poured out as a libation upon the sacrifice of the faithful; at the Holy Qurbono Christ's own sacrifice is offered, and our lives, poured out in love, are joined to it.

2027-05-13.title: Mar Ishaq Malpan of Antioch · St Isaac of Antioch · Thursday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: God's promise and oath; hope, a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul
“Let anyone who is thirsty come to me”: rivers of living water, the Spirit
2027-05-13.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Mar Ishaq Malpan of Antioch (St Isaac of Antioch).
2027-05-13.verse: We have this hope, a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul
theo: One week ago, on Suloko, we watched the Lord go up from the Mount of Olives; three days from now, at Pentecost, we shall celebrate the coming of the Spirit. Today's Gospel stands exactly between those two feasts. It is the last and greatest day of the feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem. Each morning of that feast the priests carried water from the pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, praying for the rains of the coming year. And on that day, the Gospel says, “while Jesus was standing there, he cried out, ‘Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink. As the scripture has said, “Out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water.”’” Then St John explains: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which believers in him were to receive; for as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus was not yet glorified.” This last line describes the very days we are living in the calendar. Jesus has now been glorified: he has died, risen and ascended to the Father. The rivers are about to flow. St Augustine says that we come to this fountain not with our feet but with our love: we come by desiring, by believing, by thirsting (Tractates on John 32, in substance). These ten days are given to the Church to make her thirst.

Today our Church remembers a Syriac teacher who knew this thirst: Mar Ishaq Malpan of Antioch, St Isaac of Antioch. He lived in the fifth century, and Syriac tradition remembers him as a priest and a poet who wrote long metrical homilies, memre, to be sung and recited in church. His poems speak of prayer and watchfulness, of repentance and the fear of God, of the struggle of the monk and the hope of the sinner. Scholars note that the writings of more than one Syriac Isaac have been gathered under his name, so the details of his life are uncertain; what is certain is that the Syriac Churches have treasured his verse as a school of prayer. That is why our Church gives him the title Malpan, teacher. He belongs to the great company of those who, after St Ephrem, taught the faith not only in prose but in song, so that the people could carry the teaching of the Church home on their lips. Our own Shehimo and the hymns of the Holy Qurbono are the fruit of that school.

The Letter to the Hebrews gives us the word that holds these waiting days together: hope. “When God made a promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself.” Abraham, “having patiently endured, obtained the promise.” God bound himself by promise and by oath, “so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible that God would prove false, we who have taken refuge might be strongly encouraged to seize the hope set before us.” Then comes one of the most beautiful images in the Bible: “We have this hope, a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters the inner shrine behind the curtain, where Jesus, a forerunner on our behalf, has entered, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” An anchor is thrown out of sight, below the waves, and holds the ship steady in the storm. Our anchor is thrown upward, into heaven, where the ascended Christ has gone before us. In the Holy Qurbono, when the curtain of the sanctuary opens, we glimpse that inner shrine. The forerunner is there, interceding for us, and from there he will send the Spirit like rivers of water on the thirsty land.
fathers: St Augustine

Jesus cries out: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me. Let us come, not by walking but by loving; not with the feet but with the affections of the heart; and from within us shall flow the river of the Spirit (Tractates on the Gospel of John 32, in substance).
St Ephrem the Syrian

In your Bread is hidden the Spirit who is not consumed; in your Wine dwells the Fire that is not drunk. The Spirit in your Bread, the Fire in your Wine: a wonder that our lips receive (Hymns on Faith 10, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1817

Hope is the theological virtue by which we desire the kingdom of heaven and eternal life as our happiness, placing our trust in Christ's promises and relying not on our own strength, but on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 1820

Christian hope unfolds from the beginning of Jesus' preaching; it is, in the words of Hebrews, “a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul... that enters... where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf” (in substance).
Catechism 694

The symbolism of water signifies the Holy Spirit's action in Baptism; the Spirit is also personally the living water welling up from Christ crucified as its source and welling up in us to eternal life (in substance).
outline: Opening
Ask: what is my soul thirsty for in these days?
Point 1 · God has sworn by himself
A promise and an oath that cannot fail.
Point 2 · An anchor behind the curtain
Hope thrown upward, where Christ the forerunner has gone.
Point 3 · Rivers of living water
Jesus glorified, the Spirit about to flow; Mar Ishaq's school of prayer.
Take-home line
“We have this hope, a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul.”
live: Let anyone who is thirsty come (John 7:37)
Each morning until Pentecost, drink your first glass of water slowly and pray, “Lord, give me your Spirit.”
Seize the hope set before us (Hebrews 6:18)
Write down one promise of God from Scripture and keep it in your purse or phone cover; read it when you are anxious.
2027-05-13.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, our forerunner, you have entered the inner shrine behind the curtain, and there you live for ever to intercede for us. Make our hope a sure and steadfast anchor, fixed in you and in the promise of the Father that cannot fail. You cried out, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me”: we come thirsty in these days of waiting. Pour out upon us the Holy Spirit like rivers of living water, as you promised. By the prayers of your holy Mother, who waited in the upper room with your apostles, and of Mar Ishaq Malpan, who taught your Church to pray in song, keep us watchful, repentant and full of hope. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The Fathers saw the Spirit hidden in the Bread and the Fire in the Cup; at the Holy Qurbono the glorified Christ gives himself to us, and from his pierced side the living water flows into our hearts.

2027-05-14.title: Mar Addai Shleeha · St Addai the Apostle of Edessa · Friday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: I have learned to be content; I can do all things through him who strengthens me
What is whispered will be proclaimed from the housetops; do not be afraid
2027-05-14.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the feast of Mar Addai Shleeha, the apostle of Edessa.
2027-05-14.verse: Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.
theo: Today our Church keeps the feast of Mar Addai Shleeha, and with him we stand at the very fountain of our own Syriac Christian tradition. The story is told by Eusebius of Caesarea, the first great historian of the Church, who says he found it in the archives of Edessa, written in Syriac (Church History 1.13). Abgar, the king of Edessa, a city in the north of Mesopotamia, was gravely ill. He had heard of the healings worked by Jesus, and he sent a letter asking him to come. The answer came that the Lord must first fulfil his mission, but that after he had been taken up he would send one of his disciples. “After the Ascension of Jesus,” Eusebius writes, Judas Thomas, one of the Twelve, sent Thaddaeus, one of the Seventy, to Edessa as herald and evangelist (in substance). The Syriac Churches know this Thaddaeus as Addai. He healed the king, preached Christ crucified and risen, and gathered the first Church of Edessa, which handed on its faith to his disciples Aggai and Mari. Historians judge that the letters themselves belong to legend; but behind the legend stands a fact: from the earliest generations Edessa was a Christian city, and from it the Syriac-speaking Church spread east and south. For us there is a further thread. The same tradition that sends Addai to Edessa sends Thomas to India, and it was in the Syriac world of Edessa that the story of Thomas the Apostle of India was first written down. Mar Addai is a brother in the family tree of our own faith.

Notice when Addai was sent: after the Ascension. That is the season we are in. Before he went up, the Lord told his disciples that repentance and the forgiveness of sins were to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, “beginning from Jerusalem,” and that they would be his witnesses “to the ends of the earth.” The Gospel today shows the courage that such witness needs. Jesus says: “Nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered... what you have whispered behind closed doors will be proclaimed from the housetops.” What the apostles heard quietly in the upper room was meant to be shouted in the streets of Jerusalem and Edessa and Kodungallur. Then he says, “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.” And he gives the reason, in one of the tenderest pictures in the Gospel: “Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten in God's sight. But even the hairs of your head are all counted. Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.” The missionary is not brave because he is strong, but because he knows he is counted, hair by hair, in the hands of the Father.

St Paul shows the other side of mission: the support of the Church at home. From prison he thanks the Philippians for their gift: “I rejoice in the Lord greatly that now at last you have revived your concern for me.” He wants them to know that he does not depend on comfort: “I have learned to be content with whatever I have. I know what it is to have little, and I know what it is to have plenty... I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” And yet he adds, with gratitude, “it was kind of you to share my distress.” The Philippians could not travel with Paul, but they shared in his mission by prayer and by giving. St Augustine turned this strength into a prayer: “Give what you command, and command what you will” (Confessions 10.29, in substance). On the feast of an apostle who was sent, we who stay at home are asked two things: to speak of Christ without fear in our own place, and to share the distress of those who carry him further. In two days the Spirit of Pentecost will come to make both possible.
conn: Sent after the Ascension.
Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8, with Eusebius, Church History 1.13: the Lord's command to witness to the ends of the earth is carried to Edessa by Addai, sent by Thomas after the Ascension.
From the housetops.
Luke 12:3 and Matthew 10:27: what the disciples hear in private they are to proclaim openly; the apostles of the East carried that word across the frontier of Rome.
Sharing the missionary's distress.
Philippians 4:14 and Luke 10:7: the labourer deserves to be supported; the whole Church shares in mission by prayer and gifts.
fathers: Eusebius of Caesarea

After the Ascension of Jesus, Judas, who is also called Thomas, sent to Edessa Thaddaeus, one of the Seventy, as a herald and evangelist of the teaching about Christ; and through him the words of our Saviour to King Abgar were fulfilled (Church History 1.13, in substance).
St Augustine
All my hope is in your great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will (Confessions 10.29, in substance).
magis: Ad Gentes 2

The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature, since it is from the mission of the Son and the mission of the Holy Spirit that she draws her origin, in accordance with the decree of God the Father (in substance).
Catechism 849

Having been divinely sent to the nations that she might be the universal sacrament of salvation, the Church strives to preach the Gospel to all men, in obedience to the command of her Founder (in substance).
Catechism 1808
Fortitude is the moral virtue that ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good; it enables one to conquer fear, even fear of death, and to face trials and persecutions.
outline: Opening
Ask: what have I heard about Jesus in private that I have never said aloud?
Point 1 · Sent after the Ascension
Addai, Thomas and the faith of Edessa, our own family tree.
Point 2 · Do not be afraid
Five sparrows and the counted hairs of our heads.
Point 3 · Sharing the distress of the sent
Paul's contentment and the Philippians' gift.
Take-home line
“Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.”
live: Proclaimed from the housetops (Luke 12:3)
Tell one person this week, simply and without preaching, what Jesus means to you.
Kind of you to share my distress (Philippians 4:14)
Write to, call or support a missionary priest or sister from your parish or eparchy before Pentecost.
2027-05-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, after your Ascension you sent your apostles to the ends of the earth, and through Mar Addai Shleeha you brought the light of the Gospel to Edessa and to the Syriac-speaking peoples. We thank you for the faith that came to us from the apostles, through Mar Thoma and the Church of our fathers. Take away our fear of those who can harm only the body, and teach us that we are counted in your hands, more precious than many sparrows. Give us the contentment of St Paul and his strength in you, and make us generous in sharing the distress of those who carry your name to others. By the prayers of your holy Mother and of Mar Addai, send your Holy Spirit upon your Church, and make us your witnesses where we live. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The ancient Syriac Churches pray an anaphora that bears the names of Addai and Mari; at every Holy Qurbono, in whatever tradition, the Church offers the same sacrifice that the apostles handed on, and we receive the strength to witness without fear.

2027-05-15.title: The Holy Mother of God for the ears of grain · Mar Pachomios · Saturday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: The one who sows bountifully will reap bountifully; God loves a cheerful giver
“Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
2027-05-15.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the commemoration of the Holy Mother of God for the ears of grain, the memory of Mar Pachomios (St Pachomius of Egypt), and the name day of Most Rev. Mathews Mar Pachomios. Tomorrow is Pentecost.
2027-05-15.verse: Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!
theo: On the last day before Pentecost, with the Church gathered in prayer as the apostles were gathered with Mary, the Panchangam turns our eyes to the Mother of God, and it does so in the language of the fields. Today is the commemoration of the Holy Mother of God “for the ears of grain.” In the old farming year of the Syriac lands the wheat was coming to the ear in May, and the Church brought the coming harvest to the Mother of the Lord and asked her prayers. (The Syriac calendars know other such days in the farmer's year, for the seed that is sown and for the vines; our Panchangam keeps today's.) This is not a pious decoration on the calendar. It springs from the heart of our faith. The Fathers of the Syriac Church loved to call Mary the field that was never sown, yet brought forth the Sheaf of blessing: the Virgin earth from which sprang the Bread of life. St Ephrem sings of her as the land that gave us the Wheat which feeds the world (Hymns on the Nativity, in substance). Jesus himself spoke of the grain: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” He was born in Bethlehem, whose name means “house of bread”; he gives himself as bread at every Holy Qurbono. When we remember the ears of grain in May, we remember the Mother who gave the world its true Bread.

The Gospel might seem at first to turn away from Mary. A woman in the crowd cries out, “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!” And Jesus answers, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” But the Lord is not lessening his Mother; he is telling us where her true greatness lies. St Augustine says that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (On Holy Virginity 3, in substance). She was the first to hear the word and keep it: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” She “treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart.” Elizabeth had already said of her, “blessed is she who believed.” The Second Vatican Council reads this very Gospel so: when Jesus proclaimed blessed those who hear and keep the word of God, Mary was faithfully doing just that (Lumen Gentium 58). So the woman in the crowd was right, and Jesus made her blessing deeper. Every one of us can share in the blessedness of the Mother, not by bearing Christ in the flesh, but by bearing his word in a believing heart. And tonight, on the eve of Pentecost, we wait with her, who “aided the beginnings of the Church by her prayers.”

St Paul's words to the Corinthians speak the farmer's language too. He is gathering a collection for the poor Christians of Jerusalem, and he writes: “the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. Each of you must give as you have made up your mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” Then he praises the Lord of every harvest: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.” The Panchangam also remembers today Mar Pachomios, St Pachomius of Egypt, who lived in the fourth century. As a young conscript held in a prison in Thebes, he was astonished when strangers came at night with bread and water for the prisoners. They were Christians. He promised God that if he were released he would serve others in the same way. He was baptised, learned the life of prayer from an old hermit, and gathered the first great communities of monks who lived, prayed, worked the land and shared everything in common. A cheerful gift of bread made a saint, and the saint made thousands of brothers. We pray today too for Most Rev. Mathews Mar Pachomios, a bishop of our Church, on his name day, that he may sow bountifully and reap a harvest of righteousness among God's people. Tomorrow the great Harvest begins: the Spirit will come down, and the apostles will gather in the first sheaves of the Church.
conn: The field that bore the Bread.
John 12:24 and John 6:35, with the Syriac Fathers: Christ the grain of wheat and the Bread of life came forth from the Virgin, the field that was never sown.
Hearing and keeping.
Luke 11:28 with Luke 1:38, 1:45 and 2:19: Mary is blessed above all because she heard the word of God and kept it.
Sowing and reaping.
2 Corinthians 9:6 with Psalm 126:5–6 and Galatians 6:9: the generous sower shares in God's own harvest.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian
Blessed is the Virgin earth that was never sown, yet brought forth the Sheaf of blessing; from her came the Wheat that feeds the hungry world (Hymns on the Nativity, in substance).
St Augustine

Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ; her motherhood would have profited her nothing had she not borne Christ more happily in her heart than in her flesh (On Holy Virginity 3, in substance).
magis: Lumen Gentium 58

In the course of her Son's preaching, Mary received the words by which, raising the Kingdom above ties of flesh and blood, he proclaimed blessed those who hear and keep the word of God, as she was faithfully doing (in substance).
Catechism 965

After her Son's Ascension, Mary aided the beginnings of the Church by her prayers; in her association with the apostles and several women, we also see Mary by her prayers imploring the gift of the Spirit.
Catechism 2402
In the beginning God entrusted the earth and its resources to the common stewardship of mankind; the goods of creation are destined for the whole human race (in substance).
outline: Opening
Ask: what harvest is God preparing in my life, and what seed am I sowing?
Point 1 · The field that bore the Bread
The Mother of God and the ears of grain.
Point 2 · Blessed rather
Mary, the first who heard the word and kept it.
Point 3 · The cheerful giver
Paul's harvest of righteousness and the bread that made St Pachomius a monk.
Take-home line
“Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
live: God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7)
Before tomorrow's Holy Qurbono, set aside a gift of food or money for someone in need, and give it gladly.
Hear the word of God and obey it (Luke 11:28)
Tonight, on the eve of Pentecost, read Acts 1:12–14 and 2:1–4 slowly as a family, and choose one word to keep.
2027-05-15.prayer: Lord God, Father of all good gifts, you supply seed to the sower and bread for food, and from the Virgin Mary, the field that was never sown, you gave us your Son, the Bread of life. On this commemoration of the Holy Mother of God for the ears of grain, we bring you the fields of our land and the work of all who farm them; bless the coming harvest and let no one go hungry. Make us like the Mother of your Son, who heard your word and kept it, and teach us to sow bountifully and give cheerfully, as Mar Pachomios learned from the strangers who brought him bread. Bless Most Rev. Mathews Mar Pachomios on his name day, and keep him a faithful shepherd. As we wait with Mary for the coming of your Spirit, gather us into the harvest of your Kingdom. Through Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever. Amen.
altar: The wheat of our fields becomes the bread of the altar, and by the descent of the Holy Spirit it becomes the Body of the Lord, born of the Virgin Mother of God: the true Bread from the field that was never sown.

2027-05-17.title: Monday after the Sunday of Pentecost
readings: Live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ
The Twelve are sent: “You received without payment; give without payment”
2027-05-17.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sunday of Pentecost. The season of Pentecost begins: the ten days of waiting are over, and the Church that received the Spirit is sent out.
2027-05-17.verse: Only, live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ
theo: Yesterday the Church kept Pentecost, and today the Panchangam opens a new page with a new heading: the season of Pentecost. For ten days after the Ascension the Church waited, as the apostles waited in the upper room with the Mother of Jesus; in those days our Panchangam even asks that weddings not be celebrated. Now the waiting is over. The Spirit has come, and a Church that has received the Spirit cannot stay indoors. The first weekday of the new season gives us two readings that answer one question: what does a life filled with the Spirit look like on an ordinary Monday? St Paul answers from prison, writing to the Christians of Philippi: “Only, live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent and hear about you, I will know that you are standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel, and are in no way intimidated by your opponents.” Philippi was a Roman colony, proud of its citizenship, and the verb Paul uses for “live your life” is the verb for living as a citizen. He is saying: you belong to a city whose king is Christ; let your conduct show your true citizenship.

In the Gospel Jesus sends out the Twelve for the first time, and his instructions are startling. “Go nowhere among the Gentiles, and enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” This is not a narrowing of God's love. God keeps faith with the people he chose first, and the good news goes to them first; after the Resurrection the same Lord will send the same apostles to “all nations.” Then comes their task: “As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’ Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. You received without payment; give without payment.” And their luggage: “Take no gold, or silver, or copper in your belts, no bag for your journey, or two tunics, or sandals, or a staff.” St John Chrysostom comments that the Lord stripped them of every resource so that the power that worked through them would plainly be his, and so that their poverty itself would preach (Homilies on Matthew 32, in substance). They are to enter a house with a greeting of peace, and if the house is worthy, their peace will rest upon it. Even our Holy Qurbono keeps this pattern: again and again the priest turns to the people and gives them the peace, and the Church goes out from the altar carrying it.

Paul adds a word that we would rather not hear: “For he has graciously granted you the privilege not only of believing in Christ, but of suffering for him as well.” A Spirit-filled life is not a life without opponents; it is a life that is not frightened by them. The Spirit who came at Pentecost did not remove the apostles from danger; he took away their fear. So the new season begins with a simple examination. Am I living as a citizen of Christ's kingdom at my desk, in my kitchen, on my phone? Am I standing side by side with my parish, or standing apart and criticising? What have I received without payment: faith, Baptism, the Holy Qurbono, a family that taught me to pray? And to whom am I giving it without payment? The gifts of the Spirit are not trophies for the cupboard. They are given to be handed on, at no cost, to the next person who needs them.
outline: Opening
Ask: what has the Spirit given me that I have kept to myself?
Point 1 · Citizens worthy of the gospel
Living in a way that shows whose city we belong to.
Point 2 · Side by side, not afraid
One spirit, one mind, and courage before opponents.
Point 3 · Received as gift, given as gift
The Twelve sent out with empty belts and full hands.
Take-home line
“You received without payment; give without payment.”
live: Give without payment (Matthew 10:8)
Do one service this week for which you will receive nothing, not even thanks: a visit, a repair, a lesson, an hour of listening.
Side by side (Philippians 1:27)
Instead of criticising one parish group or ministry, offer to help it for one month.
2027-05-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, yesterday you poured out your Holy Spirit on your Church, and today you send us out as you sent the Twelve. Make our lives worthy of your gospel, so that all who see us may know whose kingdom we belong to. Keep us standing firm in one spirit and striving side by side for the faith, unafraid of those who oppose us. What we have received from you without payment, let us give without payment, and let your peace rest on every house we enter. With your Father and your Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: Every gift we bring to the altar was first given to us. In the Holy Qurbono the Lord gives himself without price, and sends us out to give in the same way.

2027-05-18.title: Tuesday after the Sunday of Pentecost
readings: He shared our flesh and blood, to be a merciful and faithful high priest
The woman who lights a lamp and searches for the lost coin
2027-05-18.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sunday of Pentecost.
2027-05-18.verse: Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested.
theo: Two short readings today tell one story from two sides: how far God was willing to come to find us. The Letter to the Hebrews begins with a plain fact about us: “the children share flesh and blood.” We are bodies that get tired, fall ill, grow old and die. Then it tells us what the Son of God did about it: “he himself likewise shared the same things, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil.” He did not rescue us from a distance, like a ship that throws a rope and sails on. He came on board. He took a body from the Virgin Mary, the same flesh and blood as ours, so that death, the one thing we all share, could become the place where he met the enemy and defeated him. “For it is clear that he did not come to help angels, but the descendants of Abraham.” God's mercy is not for some other, cleaner kind of creature. It is for us, the children of Abraham's faith, with our weak bodies and our anxious hearts.

From this Hebrews draws a conclusion that is full of comfort: “Therefore he had to become like his brothers and sisters in every respect, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make a sacrifice of atonement for the sins of the people. Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested.” Our High Priest is not a stranger to temptation, hunger, betrayal or grief. When we bring him our struggle, we are not explaining something he cannot imagine; we are speaking to someone who has been there. In the Gospel the same mercy wears an everyday face. “Or what woman having ten silver coins, if she loses one of them, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?” A silver coin of that kind was roughly a day's wage, and for a poor household one coin mattered. The house is dark, the floor is earth, and the coin is somewhere in the dust. She does not shrug and say she still has nine. She lights a lamp, she sweeps, she searches until she finds it.

St Gregory the Great read this parable as a picture of the Incarnation: the woman is the Wisdom of God, and the lamp she lights is light in a clay vessel, the divinity of the Son shining in our flesh; with it she sweeps the house of our conscience until the lost image of God is found again (Homilies on the Gospels 34, in substance). The coin, after all, bears an image, and we were made in God's image. That image can be buried in dust, but it is never erased. The parable ends in a party: “When she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” In this season of Pentecost, the Spirit is the lamp and the broom in the hands of the Church. Is there someone you have written off as lost, a relative, a former friend, a young person who has stopped coming to church? Do not say there are still nine. Light a lamp: pray. Sweep: make the first move. Search carefully: keep looking until the coin is found. And if you are the lost coin today, know that you are being searched for, and come to the sacrament of Confession, where heaven's joy begins.
outline: Opening
Ask: whom have I quietly given up on as lost?
Point 1 · He shared our flesh and blood
The Son came on board and met death from the inside.
Point 2 · A merciful and faithful high priest
Tested like us, so that he can help us when we are tested.
Point 3 · Light a lamp, sweep, search
The woman who will not settle for nine coins.
Take-home line
“He is able to help those who are being tested.”
live: Bring him the test (Hebrews 2:18)
Name the temptation or trial that weighs on you most, and speak to Jesus about it in your own words every evening this week.
Search for one coin (Luke 15:8)
Contact one person who has drifted away from you or from the Church, without preaching: simply show that you care.
2027-05-18.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you shared our flesh and blood and through your death you destroyed the power of the one who held us in fear. You became like us in every respect, a merciful and faithful High Priest, tested as we are tested. Help us in our hour of trial. Like the woman who lit a lamp and swept her house, you search for every one of us who is lost. By your Holy Spirit make us lamps in your hands, to seek out those who have strayed and to rejoice with heaven over every sinner who returns. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The High Priest who shared our flesh and blood now gives us his own Body and Blood. In the Holy Qurbono the one who searched for us feeds us when we are found.

2027-05-19.title: Memory of Mar Yaqob Shleeha's first offering of the Holy Qurbono · Wednesday after the Sunday of Pentecost
readings: “Do this in remembrance of me”: the Lord's Supper handed on
“I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you”
2027-05-19.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sunday of Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of the first offering of the Holy Qurbono by Mar Yaqob Shleeha. Which James is meant is not stated; our Syriac tradition honours St James, “the Lord's brother” and first bishop of Jerusalem, as the one to whom the Anaphora of St James is ascribed.
2027-05-19.verse: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.
theo: Three days after Pentecost our Church keeps a memory that belongs to her very heart: the memory of Mar Yaqob Shleeha offering the Holy Qurbono for the first time. The Panchangam does not say which James is meant, but our Syriac tradition has always looked to St James of Jerusalem, called by St Paul “James the Lord's brother,” that is, a close kinsman of Jesus. The risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7); he led the Church of Jerusalem and spoke decisively at the council of the apostles (Acts 15:13–21); ancient writers remember him as the first bishop of that city and tell of a man of such prayer that his knees grew hard as a camel's (Hegesippus, in Eusebius, Church History 2.23, in substance). He was put to death in Jerusalem about the year 62. To him the tradition ascribes the Anaphora of St James, the great Eucharistic prayer of the Church of Jerusalem, which became the pattern of the West Syriac Qurbono that we celebrate. We cannot date the morning when he first stood at the altar. But we know what the memory means: from the first days after Pentecost, the Church that had received the Spirit gathered for “the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42), doing what the Lord had commanded.

The Epistle gives us the oldest written account of that command. Writing to Corinth some twenty years after the Resurrection, St Paul says: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, ‘This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ In the same way he took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’” Received and handed on: that is how the Qurbono reached us, from the upper room to Jerusalem, from Jerusalem to Antioch, from Antioch to the shores of Kerala, from one generation of priests and faithful to the next. In the Gospel St Luke lets us hear the longing in the Lord's voice: “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” The Supper is not something the disciples arranged for Jesus; it is something he longed to give them. “This is my body, which is given for you.” “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”

St Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching the newly baptised in the very city of St James, told them not to regard the bread and wine as plain bread and wine, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ according to the Lord's own word; even if the senses suggest otherwise, let faith make you sure (Mystagogical Catecheses 4.6, in substance). This is the faith of the Catholic Church: in the Holy Qurbono the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present, and Christ, true God and true man, is truly, really and substantially present under the forms of bread and wine. “Remembrance” here is not a fond memory of something absent; it is the living memorial in which the Lord's sacrifice becomes present to us. And it looks forward too: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.” Today let us thank God for every priest who has stood at the altar for us, from St James to the young priest of our own parish. Let us come to the Qurbono not as spectators but as those whom the Lord eagerly desired to feed. And if we have grown careless, arriving late, leaving early, receiving without preparation, let this memory of the first Qurbono make our next one feel like the first again.
conn: The blood of the covenant.
Exodus 24:8 and Luke 22:20: Moses sealed the covenant at Sinai with the blood of sacrifice; Jesus gives the cup of the new covenant in his own blood, as Jeremiah 31:31 had promised.
The pure offering in every place.

Malachi 1:11: from the rising of the sun to its setting a pure offering is made to God's name; from the Didache onward the Church has seen this fulfilled in the Eucharist offered among all the nations.
The Passover fulfilled.
Exodus 12:14 and Luke 22:15–16: the Passover was a day of remembrance for ever; Jesus eats it with longing and fulfils it in the kingdom of God.
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem

Do not regard the bread and wine as plain and ordinary, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ, as the Lord himself has declared; though the senses suggest otherwise, let faith establish you (Mystagogical Catecheses 4.6, in substance).
St Ignatius of Antioch

Some keep away from the Eucharist and from prayer because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised up (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7, in substance).
The Didache

On the Lord's day gather, break bread and give thanks, having first confessed your sins, so that your sacrifice may be pure, as the Lord said: in every place offer me a pure sacrifice (Didache 14, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1324
The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life”; all the sacraments and ministries of the Church are bound up with it and directed towards it.
Catechism 1366
The Eucharist is a sacrifice because it re-presents, makes present, the sacrifice of the Cross, is its memorial and applies its fruit.
Catechism 1374
In the Most Blessed Sacrament the Body and Blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the whole Christ, is truly, really and substantially contained.
Catechism 1203

The liturgical traditions in use in the Church include the Latin and the Byzantine, Alexandrian or Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite and Chaldean rites; the Church holds all of them to be of equal right and dignity.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did the Holy Qurbono last feel to me like the first time?
Point 1 · Received and handed on
From the upper room through St James to our own altar.
Point 2 · Eagerly desired
The Lord longs to give himself to us.
Point 3 · Until he comes
The memorial that makes his sacrifice present and looks to his coming.
Take-home line
“Do this in remembrance of me.”
live: Prepare for the Qurbono (1 Corinthians 11:26)
Arrive ten minutes early at your next Holy Qurbono and spend the time in silence before the altar.
Thank a priest (Luke 22:19)
Write a short note or say a word of thanks to a priest who has offered the Qurbono for you, and pray for him by name.
2027-05-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on the night you were betrayed you took bread and the cup and gave them to your apostles as your Body and Blood, and you commanded, Do this in remembrance of me. We thank you for Mar Yaqob Shleeha and for all who have offered the Holy Qurbono from the first days of your Church until now. As you eagerly desired to eat the Passover with your disciples, give us a hunger for your holy Mysteries. Make us worthy to receive them with faith and love, to proclaim your death and Resurrection, and to wait for your coming in glory. With your Father and your Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: Today the altar itself is the feast. What Mar Yaqob offered in Jerusalem, our priest offers in our parish: the one sacrifice of Christ, made present for us until he comes.

2027-05-20.title: The Four Evangelists · Thursday after the Sunday of Pentecost
readings: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”; faith comes from what is heard
“Go therefore and make disciples of all nations”; “I am with you always”
2027-05-20.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sunday of Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the commemoration of the Four Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
2027-05-20.verse: So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
theo: In the first week of the season of Pentecost our Church gathers four saints into one feast: the Four Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, through whose writing the good news of Jesus reaches every generation. Matthew was the tax collector whom Jesus called from his booth (Matthew 9:9). Mark, ancient writers tell us, set down the preaching of St Peter, whose interpreter he had been (Papias, in Eusebius, Church History 3.39, in substance). Luke was the physician and companion of St Paul (Colossians 4:14), who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles. John is the disciple whom Jesus loved, who “has testified to these things and has written them” (John 21:24). Four men, four styles, four points of view, and one Lord. St Irenaeus, writing in the second century, already insisted that the Gospel is fourfold and yet one, held together by one Spirit, like the four winds or the four pillars of a single house (Against Heresies 3.11.8, in substance). The Church gave each evangelist a sign from the four living creatures that Ezekiel saw around the throne of God: the human face for Matthew, the lion for Mark, the ox for Luke, the eagle for John.

The Epistle explains why the evangelists matter. St Paul builds a chain of questions: “But how are they to call on one in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in one of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim him? And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!’” Then the conclusion: “So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.” Nobody invents faith for himself. It comes by hearing, and we hear because someone was sent and someone wrote. Paul goes on to speak with sorrow and hope of his own people Israel, who had heard and not yet believed; elsewhere he insists that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). He also applies to the preachers a line from the psalm about the heavens: “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” The four Gospels are that voice. They have gone out in hundreds of languages; in our own Syriac tradition the Gospels were read for some centuries in a single woven harmony, until in the fifth century bishops such as Rabbula of Edessa saw to it that the four separate Gospels were read in the churches. Today they are read in Malayalam at our altars.

The Gospel is the last page of St Matthew. The eleven go to the mountain in Galilee: “When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.” Even at the end, the evangelist is honest about the disciples' weakness. Jesus does not wait for their doubts to vanish. He comes near and gives them everything: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything that I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” He is with us in the Holy Qurbono, and he is with us in the word. That is why, in our Qurbono, the Gospel is not simply read like a notice: it is called the Evangelion, it is proclaimed by the priest, and the people stand to hear the Lord himself speak. St Jerome said that ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ (Commentary on Isaiah, prologue, in substance). On this feast, take one of the four Gospels and begin to read it through, a chapter a day. Mark can be read in under three weeks. Let the evangelists do for you what they have done for the whole Church: bring you face to face with Jesus.
conn: The four living creatures.

Ezekiel 1:10 and Revelation 4:7: the faces of a human being, a lion, an ox and an eagle around God's throne; from St Irenaeus and St Jerome onward the Church has read them as signs of the four Gospels.
Beautiful feet.
Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15: the prophet's messenger running over the mountains with good news becomes every preacher of the Gospel.
Their voice to all the earth.
Psalm 19:4 and Romans 10:18: the silent preaching of the heavens becomes the preaching of the apostles and evangelists to the ends of the world.
fathers: St Irenaeus

It is not possible that the Gospels should be more or fewer than four: as there are four zones of the world and four principal winds, the Church has four pillars, and the Word has given us the Gospel under four aspects but bound together by one Spirit (Against Heresies 3.11.8, in substance).
St Jerome
The first face, of a man, signifies Matthew; the second, of a lion, Mark; the third, of a calf, Luke; the fourth, of an eagle, John (Commentary on Matthew, preface, in substance).
St Jerome
Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ (Commentary on Isaiah, prologue, in substance).
magis: Dei Verbum 18
Among all the Scriptures, even those of the New Testament, the Gospels have a special preeminence, for they are the principal witness to the life and teaching of the incarnate Word, our Saviour.
Dei Verbum 19
Holy Mother Church has firmly held, and continues to hold, that the four Gospels faithfully hand on what Jesus, while living among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.
Catechism 127
The fourfold Gospel holds a unique place in the Church, as is evident both in the veneration the liturgy accords it and in the surpassing attraction it has exercised on the saints at all times.
Catechism 849

The missionary mandate: having been divinely sent to the nations to be the universal sacrament of salvation, the Church strives to preach the Gospel to all, in obedience to the command of her Founder.
outline: Opening
Ask: which Gospel have I actually read from beginning to end?
Point 1 · Four voices, one Gospel
Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, bound together by one Spirit.
Point 2 · Faith comes from what is heard
Sent, proclaimed, heard, believed.
Point 3 · Go and make disciples
The Lord with us always, in the Qurbono and in the word.
Take-home line
“Faith comes from what is heard.”
live: Read a Gospel through (Romans 10:17)
Begin today to read the Gospel of Mark, one chapter a day, until you finish it.
Beautiful feet (Romans 10:15)
Share one Gospel passage that has helped you with someone who needs encouragement this week.
2027-05-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, living Word of the Father, you gave your Church the four holy Gospels through Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, so that all who hear may believe and have life in your name. We thank you for the evangelists and for all who have handed on your word in every language, and in ours. Open our ears to hear you, our hearts to believe, and our lips to proclaim you. Send us, as you sent the eleven, to make disciples, and keep your promise to be with us always, to the end of the age. With your Father and your Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Lord sets two tables before us: the table of the word, where the Evangelion is proclaimed, and the table of his Body and Blood. The evangelists serve at the first, so that we may come to the second with faith.

2027-05-21.title: Golden Friday · the first Friday after Pentecost · St Helena the Queen
readings: “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you”: the lame man at the Beautiful Gate
If I do not have love, I am nothing
The camel and the eye of a needle; “for God all things are possible”
2027-05-21.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sunday of Pentecost. Golden Friday (സ്വർണ്ണ വെള്ളിയാഴ്ച), the first Friday after Pentecost, remembers the first miracle the apostles worked in the name of Jesus after receiving the Holy Spirit. The Panchangam also remembers St Helena the Queen. Today has three readings: Acts, Epistle and Gospel.
2027-05-21.verse: I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.
theo: On the first Friday after Pentecost our Church keeps a day with a beautiful name: Golden Friday. It remembers the first miracle that the apostles worked in the name of Jesus after the Holy Spirit came upon them, the healing of the man lame from birth at the gate of the temple called the Beautiful Gate. The name is usually explained from St Peter's own words that day: “I have no silver or gold.” The Church has no gold to give, and yet the day is golden, because what Peter had was worth more than all the gold of the temple. Five days after Pentecost, the readings set before us three kinds of wealth: the power of the name of Jesus in Acts, the gold of love in St Paul, and the treasure in heaven of those who leave everything in the Gospel. And the Panchangam joins to them the memory of St Helena, a queen who had all the gold of an empire at her disposal and spent it for Christ. One with no gold heals; one with much gold gives. Both show that the only wealth that lasts is the wealth that is placed in the hands of Jesus.

The story in Acts is told with great care. “One day Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, at three o'clock in the afternoon.” The apostles, filled with the Spirit, still keep the hours of prayer; it is the ninth hour, the hour at which our own Shehimo still calls us to pray, the hour at which the Lord died on the Cross. “And a man lame from birth was being carried in. People would lay him daily at the gate of the temple called the Beautiful Gate so that he could ask for alms from those entering the temple.” He has never stood. He lives at the edge of the holy place, at the gate but never inside. “Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, ‘Look at us.’ And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.” He expects a coin. “But Peter said, ‘I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.’ And he took him by the right hand and raised him up; and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.” St John Chrysostom remarks that the man asked for a few coins and received his feet, and with them the gift of walking into the house of God (Homilies on Acts 8, in substance). “Jumping up, he stood and began to walk, and he entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.” The prophecy of Isaiah has come true before the eyes of Jerusalem: “then the lame shall leap like a deer.” The man who sat outside the gate now goes in. That is what the name of Jesus does.

St Paul tells us where the gold of the Church really lies. “If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. If I give away all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.” Even miracles, even generosity, even martyrdom, are empty without love. Peter's miracle was not a display of power; it was love that stopped, looked, touched and lifted. “Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices in the truth.” St Augustine summed it up in a famous line: love, and do what you will; for if the root of love is within, nothing but good can grow from it (Homilies on the First Letter of John 7.8, in substance). The healing at the Beautiful Gate is the first gold of the Church after Pentecost, and it is the gold of love.

The Gospel brings the same question home. “Truly I tell you, it will be hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.” The disciples are astounded: “Then who can be saved?” Jesus looks at them: “For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.” Then Peter speaks, the same Peter who will one day say at the Beautiful Gate that he has no silver or gold: “Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?” Jesus promises a hundredfold and eternal life. Peter had left his boat and his nets; at the temple gate he discovered that he was richer than any merchant in Jerusalem. St Ambrose tells how the deacon St Lawrence, ordered to hand over the treasures of the Church, gathered the poor and said: these are the treasures of the Church (On the Duties of the Clergy 2.28, in substance). St Helena understood this too. Eusebius records that on her pilgrimage to the Holy Land, as an old woman, she built churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives and gave generously to the poor wherever she went (Life of Constantine 3.41–44, in substance). So Golden Friday asks each of us a direct question. What is my gold, and whose hands is it in? Perhaps I have no money to give; then give what you have: a hand to lift someone, a visit, a word spoken in the name of Jesus. Perhaps I have more than I need; then remember the camel and the needle, and let your wealth build up the house of God and lift up the poor. For God all things are possible, even a rich heart made poor enough to enter the kingdom.
conn: The lame shall leap.

Isaiah 35:6 and Acts 3:8: the prophet foretold that in the days of salvation the lame would leap like a deer; at the Beautiful Gate the man lame from birth goes into the temple walking and leaping and praising God.
No gold in their belts.
Matthew 10:8–9 and Acts 3:6: Jesus sent the Twelve with no gold or silver, to give without payment what they had received; Peter keeps that command and gives the man the gift of the name of Jesus.
Leaving everything.
Matthew 19:27 and Acts 3:6: Peter who said, “We have left everything and followed you,” is the Peter who says, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you.”
The greatest of these.
1 Corinthians 13:1–3 and Deuteronomy 6:5: the Law commands love of God with all one's heart; Paul shows that every gift, even miracles, is nothing without love.
fathers: St John Chrysostom

The lame man asked for a little money and received his feet; Peter gave him more than he asked, and the one who sat outside the temple went in walking and praising God (Homilies on Acts 8, in substance).
St Augustine

Love, and do what you will: if you keep silence, keep silence out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; let the root of love be within, for from that root nothing but good can spring (Homilies on the First Letter of John 7.8, in substance).
St Ambrose
When the persecutor demanded the treasures of the Church, the deacon Lawrence brought the poor and said: these are the treasures of the Church (On the Duties of the Clergy 2.28, in substance).
Eusebius of Caesarea

Though advanced in years, the empress Helena travelled to the Holy Land, adorned the places of the Lord's birth and Ascension with churches, and gave generously to the poor and needy wherever she went (Life of Constantine 3.41–44, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1507

The risen Lord renews the mission to heal (“In my name... they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover”) and confirms it through the signs that the Church performs by invoking his name.
Catechism 1826
“If I... have not charity,” says the Apostle, “I am nothing.” Whatever my privilege, service or even virtue, without charity I gain nothing.
Catechism 2544
Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and bids them renounce all that they have for his sake and that of the Gospel.
Deus Caritas Est 22
Love for widows and orphans, prisoners, and the sick and needy of every kind is as essential to the Church as the ministry of the sacraments and preaching of the Gospel.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is my gold, and whose hands is it in?
Point 1 · “I have no silver or gold”
The first miracle after Pentecost at the Beautiful Gate.
Point 2 · In the name of Jesus
The man at the gate goes in, walking and leaping.
Point 3 · The gold of love
Without love, even miracles are nothing.
Point 4 · For God all things are possible
The camel, the needle, and the hundredfold; St Helena's generosity.
Take-home line
“What I have I give you.”
live: What I have I give you (Acts 3:6)
Look intently this week at one person who sits at the gate of your life, a beggar, a neighbour in need, a lonely relative, and give what you have: time, help, a hand to lift them.
Place your gold in Christ's hands (Matthew 19:23–29)
Decide today on one concrete gift to the poor or to the Church from what you own, and give it before Sunday, quietly.
2027-05-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, after the coming of your Holy Spirit your apostles Peter and John healed the lame man at the Beautiful Gate, not with silver or gold but in your holy name. On this Golden Friday make us rich in what truly matters. Give us eyes to look intently at those who sit at the gate, hands to lift them up, and hearts full of the love without which we are nothing. Loosen our grip on what we own, so that like St Helena we may spend it for your glory and for the poor, and like your apostles leave everything to follow you. For with God all things are possible. With your Father and your Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar we receive what no gold can buy: the Body and Blood of the Lord in whose name the lame man stood up. From the Holy Qurbono we go out with something to give, in his name.

2027-05-22.title: Saturday after the Sunday of Pentecost · St Rita
readings: “You are a letter of Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God”
The wise and foolish bridesmaids: “Keep awake therefore”
2027-05-22.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sunday of Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Rita. This evening the First Sunday after Pentecost begins with Evening Prayer; its Evening Gospel is Luke 8:4–15.
2027-05-22.verse: you show that you are a letter of Christ, prepared by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
theo: At the end of the first week of the season of Pentecost, St Paul gives us a picture of what the Holy Spirit does in a Christian. Some people in Corinth had begun to ask for Paul's credentials: where were his letters of recommendation? Paul answers: “Surely we do not need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you or from you, do we? You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all; and you show that you are a letter of Christ, prepared by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.” The tablets of stone recall Sinai, where God gave the Law to Moses; the Jewish people still keep the feast of Weeks, Shavuot, in memory of that gift, and it was on that very feast that the Spirit came upon the apostles. The prophets had promised a day when God would write his law within his people: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Paul says that day has come. The Spirit of Pentecost is a writer, and his paper is the human heart.

Paul goes on: “our competence is from God, who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” This is not contempt for the Law, which Paul elsewhere calls “holy” (Romans 7:12), nor for the people to whom it was given. The Law shone with glory, so that the people “could not gaze at Moses' face because of the glory of his face.” But a commandment written outside us can only tell us what to do; it cannot give us the strength to do it. St Augustine put the difference simply: by the law of works God says, Do what I command; by the law of faith we say to God, Give what you command (On the Spirit and the Letter 13.22, in substance). The Spirit does not only show us the way; he becomes the life within us that walks in it. “How much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory?” The glory once seen on Moses' face is now meant to shine, quietly, in ordinary Christian lives, so that anyone who reads us reads Christ.

The Gospel tells us how to keep that letter legible: keep the lamp burning. Ten bridesmaids wait for the bridegroom; five take flasks of oil, five do not. “As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept.” Everyone sleeps; the difference is in the oil. When the cry comes at midnight, the foolish ask to borrow, and the wise cannot lend, because the oil of a life cannot be handed over at the last minute. St John Chrysostom saw in the oil the works of mercy, the kindness and almsgiving that keep faith burning (Homilies on Matthew 78, in substance). Today the Panchangam remembers St Rita of Cascia, a woman whose lamp burned through a long night. Born in Umbria about 1381, she was married young to a hard and violent man, and for years she answered him with patience and prayer; he changed, and then was murdered. She forgave his killers and prayed that her sons would not take revenge. After their death she entered the Augustinian monastery at Cascia, where she lived in prayer and penance until her death on 22 May 1457. Many in Kerala call on her as the patron of impossible causes. Her life was a letter written by the Spirit on a human heart, in a hand that anger and grief could not erase. Ask her prayers today for a marriage under strain, for a family divided by revenge, for a cause that looks hopeless, and keep your own lamp filled: “Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.”
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone read my life this week, what would they read about Christ?
Point 1 · A letter of Christ
Written by the Spirit on human hearts.
Point 2 · The Spirit gives life
Not only the command, but the strength to keep it.
Point 3 · Oil in the lamp
The wise bridesmaids and St Rita's long night of faith.
Take-home line
“You are a letter of Christ.”
live: Be a readable letter (2 Corinthians 3:2)
Choose one person at home or at work who finds faith hard, and let them read Christ in one concrete act of patience this week.
Fill your lamp (Matthew 25:4)
Do one work of mercy each day until next Saturday: a visit, an alms, a phone call to someone lonely.
2027-05-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, by your Holy Spirit you write your law on the tablets of our hearts and make us letters of your love for all to read. Write in us what you will. Do not let the letter of the law lie dead in us, but let your Spirit give us life and strength to do what you command. Keep our lamps filled with the oil of faith and good works, so that when you, the Bridegroom, come at midnight, we may go in with you to the wedding feast. By the prayers of St Rita, give patience to those who suffer at home, forgiveness to those who are wronged, and hope to those whose cause seems impossible. With your Father and your Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Bridegroom comes to us now, before the midnight cry. In the Holy Qurbono he fills our lamps with his own life, so that we may burn until he comes.

2027-05-24.title: Monday of the first week after Pentecost
readings: No longer strangers: built together into a dwelling place for God
They loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God
2027-05-24.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the First Sunday after Pentecost.
2027-05-24.verse: in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
theo: A week ago the Holy Spirit came down on the apostles gathered with the Mother of God in the upper room, and the Church went out into the streets of Jerusalem. Yesterday, on the First Sunday after Pentecost, we heard of the fruit the Spirit wants to grow in us. Today St Paul shows us what the Spirit is building. He is writing to Gentile Christians in Ephesus, people who had once stood outside the covenant of Israel, and he tells them who they are now: “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.” A stranger waits at the gate; a member of the household sits at the table. Every one of us came into the Church as a stranger, carried to the font as a baby or walking in as an adult, and was made a son or daughter of the house. In the Holy Qurbono we stand together before one altar, old families and new, those who sing well and those who cannot sing at all, and not one of us is a guest. The foundation is not our own merit but the faith handed on by the apostles and prophets, and the stone that holds every corner together is Christ himself.

Paul goes on: “In him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.” Behind the word “spiritually” stands Paul's phrase “in the Spirit”: it is the Holy Spirit who joins the stones. A building is not a heap. Stones lying in a quarry are only stones; fitted together, they become a house where someone can live. St Augustine, preaching at the dedication of a church, told his people that what had happened to the timber and the stone while the building went up happens to believers: they are cut from the forest and the hillside when they come to faith, shaped and squared in instruction and Baptism, and they become the house of the Lord only when they are bound together by charity (Sermon 336, in substance). That is the work of these weeks after Pentecost: the Spirit fitting us together. It can hurt to be fitted to other stones: to forgive a neighbour, to work with a difficult committee, to bear with a relative who tests our patience. But without that fitting there is no house, only a pile of stones. And the Gospel shows how a stone can hold back from being built in.

St John looks back over the public ministry of Jesus with sorrow: “Although he had performed so many signs in their presence, they did not believe in him.” He sees in this the mystery that Isaiah had already met, that the word of God can be heard and not received. Then he adds a sentence that cuts close in every age: “Nevertheless many, even of the authorities, believed in him. But because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue; for they loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God.” These people were not unbelievers. They believed, but quietly, and they would not say so, because it would cost them their place. John is not passing judgement on a whole people; he is describing a temptation as common in our towns today as in Jerusalem then. St Augustine warned, commenting on this passage, that the love of human praise can stop a person on the very threshold of faith (Tractates on John 53, in substance). How many of us believe at home and fall silent at the office, in the hostel or at the family gathering when the talk turns against the Church? Members of the household do not hide which house they belong to. Ask today for the courage to make the sign of the Cross before your meal in the canteen, to say a good word for the Church when it is not popular, to admit that you were at the Qurbono on Sunday. The Spirit who came at Pentecost turned frightened men into witnesses; he can do the same with us.
outline: Opening
Ask: where do I believe quietly but stay silent when it might cost me something?
Point 1 · No longer strangers
Baptism made us members of the household of God.
Point 2 · Built together in the Spirit
Stones become a house only when they are fitted together in love.
Point 3 · The glory that comes from God
The believers who would not confess, and the courage the Spirit gives.
Take-home line
“You also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.”
live: Be fitted to another stone (Ephesians 2:21)
Take one step this week towards a person in the parish or the family with whom you find it hard to work or to speak.
Confess him before others (John 12:42)
Make the sign of the Cross before one meal you eat in public today, quietly and without embarrassment.
2027-05-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, cornerstone of the house of God, through Baptism you made us no longer strangers but members of your household. Send your Holy Spirit to fit us together, stone with stone, in patience and in love, so that our parish and our families may become a dwelling place for God. Take from us the fear that makes us silent and the love of human praise that holds us back. Give us the courage to confess you before others and to seek only the glory that comes from the Father. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Around one altar the stones of the house are gathered: in the Holy Qurbono the Body of Christ is given to many, and the many become one body, a temple where God lives.

2027-05-25.title: Tuesday of the first week after Pentecost · St Sophia
readings: We do not lose heart; we look at what cannot be seen
The parable of the pounds: “Do business with these until I come back”
2027-05-25.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the First Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Sophia; it does not say which of the holy women of that name is meant.
2027-05-25.verse: So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.
theo: Today the Panchangam names a saint called Sophia and tells us nothing more. Several holy women of that name are honoured in the calendars of East and West, and we need not guess which one our Church has in mind. The name itself is enough to pray with. Sophia is the Greek word for wisdom, and the readings of the day are a lesson in the wisdom that looks beyond what can be seen. St Paul writes to the Corinthians from the middle of great hardship. He has been afflicted, perplexed, persecuted and struck down, and his body carries the marks. Yet he says: “So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.” Every one of us knows the outer nature that wastes away: the knees that complain on the church steps, the eyes that need stronger glasses, the strength that is not what it was. Paul does not pretend otherwise. But he sees something growing while the body declines: an inner person, renewed day by day by the Spirit who was poured out at Pentecost. Old age, illness and loss are not the end of the story for a Christian; they can be the very place where the inner person grows young.
